name: ModWatch
one_liner: Cron-fed alerts and bid-priced rate cards for federal and state prevailing-wage determinations, so a contractor never bids or pays against a superseded wage determination revision.
problem: Davis-Bacon/SCA wage determinations are revised continuously on SAM.gov (about 90,033 determinations, ~495,000 rate lines, ~128,735 location rows; only ~6% of DBA records are active at any moment — the rest are superseded revisions). Contractors must pin the correct revision at bid, re-pin it at award, and watch the FAR 22.404-6 timing rules (a modification published <10 days before bid opening, and the 90-day post-bid-opening rule that makes later mods effective). Get it wrong and DOL enforcement means back wages for every affected worker for the full violation period, withheld contract payments, up to 3-year debarment, and criminal exposure for false certification; one documented fringe-calculation error cost $13,508. Today small contractors do this by hand — 'we've got 12 guys' shops spending 2-3 hours every Friday on certified payroll — because compliance platforms (LCPtracker, eMars, Points North at ~$175+/mo with $1,500+ setup) are priced and scoped for 100+ employee companies and are demo-quoted, not self-serve. Nobody sells the narrow, high-frequency job: 'did the WD I'm bidding/performing under change, by how many dollars per hour, and what does that do to my labor line?'
target_customer: Owner-operators and estimators at 5-75 employee specialty and general contractors doing federally funded or state prevailing-wage work (electrical, mechanical, paving, roofing, drywall, low-voltage), plus their outside bookkeepers. Buying trigger is a live bid or an award; they self-identify by searching a WD number or a county+craft rate.
revenue_model: Self-serve monthly SaaS subscription (Stripe Checkout + Billing, card on file, automatic dunning and cancellation) with a one-time instant-download product as the entry offer. Tiering by number of watched wage determinations, states, and crew size — a usage metric the customer picks at signup and can upgrade in-app. Annual prepay at 2 months free. Value delivery is entirely email/Slack alerts plus generated PDFs in the app.
pricing_hypothesis: One-time 'Bid Rate Card' $49 per project (instant PDF, no account needed beyond email) as the fast first dollar; Watch $79/mo (3 active WDs, alerts + diffs); Bid $199/mo (15 WDs, crew-mix labor-cost modeling, rate cards, multi-county); Shop $499/mo (unlimited WDs, multi-state incl. CA DIR, API, unlimited seats). Ramanujam's willingness-to-pay-first logic: price the delta against a single avoided back-wage finding ($13,508 civil penalty scale), not against payroll-software seat prices — so even $499/mo is <4% of one violation.
knowledge_base: Assembled corpus: (1) SAM.gov Wage Determination API — DBA, SCA and CBA determinations with per-classification base wage and fringe, plus the county/state location rows; DOL publishes revisions on a rolling basis with a Friday cadence. No bulk download exists and the API is page-at-a-time, which is exactly the assembly work that becomes the moat: we maintain a full mirrored history of every revision with per-classification diffs, which SAM itself does not expose. (2) DOL WHD All Agency Memoranda and conformance guidance. (3) California DIR general prevailing wage determinations (issued Feb 22 and Aug 22, plus predetermined increases) and rate files for NY, WA, NJ, IL, OH. (4) SAM.gov contract-opportunities API to bind WD numbers to live solicitations. Refresh cron: 06:00 ET daily incremental poll of the WD API keyed on revision number; 02:00 ET Saturday full reconcile and rehash of the mirror; state files monthly, plus pinned jobs on Feb 22 / Aug 22 for CA DIR; opportunities hourly during business days. Staleness detection: if the max revision date across the DBA corpus has not advanced in 10 calendar days, or a nightly hash of the location table changes by >5% (a schema break), the pipeline fails closed, halts alert sends, and paints a dated 'feed may be stale' banner in every account.
autonomy_case: A1: signup is email + Stripe Checkout; the $49 rate card is purchasable before an account exists. No demo, no call — the product is a search box over public wage data, which is the acquisition channel and the onboarding. A2: everything shipped is generated — revision diffs, per-craft $/hr deltas, labor-cost impact against an uploaded crew CSV, and the rate-card PDF are all code output from the mirrored corpus; no human touches an artifact. A3: the hard case is a craft in the customer's crew with no matching classification in the WD. The engine does not guess a classification. It renders a 'no classification match' card showing the 3 nearest classifications with their scope-of-work text side by side and the similarity score, marks the rate card 'incomplete — 1 unconformed classification, cost estimate excludes it', and explains the SF-1444 conformance path in-product with a self-serve worksheet and the DOL guidance link. Second degrade: for the FAR 22.404-6 timing question it states the rule and the observable dates ('Mod 14 published 6 days before bid opening') and explicitly declines to conclude effectiveness, because that turns on a contracting-officer finding we cannot see. Third degrade: if a state feed is stale, affected watches are suppressed and the account is auto-credited for that month. Nothing routes to a person. A4: corpus refreshes on the crons above from SAM.gov's API and state DOL publications, all machine-readable, with hash-based staleness detection. A5: ingestion, diffing, alert fan-out, Stripe dunning, and uptime checks all run on schedules; every stage fails closed (no diff, no send). A6: zero human minutes per customer — support is a docs site plus an in-product answer bot grounded strictly in our own corpus and DOL text; the only inbound driver is 'why did this rate change', which is answered by the diff card itself.
time_to_first_revenue: 3-5 weeks. Week 1-2: mirror the SAM.gov WD API and build the revision-diff engine. Week 3: ship the free public WD lookup (SEO surface) plus the $49 rate-card checkout. Week 4-5: subscription watches and alerting. The $49 one-time product means revenue does not wait on the subscription.
risks: (1) Vitamin risk — alerts alone may not be a painkiller; mitigation is tying every alert to a dollar figure on the customer's own crew mix and to the bid rate card, which is what actually gets bought. (2) SAM.gov API rate limits, key policy, or ToS changes could throttle the mirror; mitigation is polite incremental polling, cached history (our history has standalone value even if the live feed degrades), and a documented fallback to the public WD web surface. (3) DOL already offers rudimentary WD email subscriptions and could improve them — but they will not produce crew-cost modeling or bid rate cards. (4) Incumbents (LCPtracker, Points North, eBacon) could bundle alerts; mitigation is Dunford-style positioning away from certified payroll entirely — we are not a payroll system, we are the rate-of-record service. (5) Buyer is price-sensitive and low-tech; mitigate with a free lookup that ranks for '[county] [craft] prevailing wage rate' long-tail queries (Weinberg & Mares: SEO as the single bullseye channel). (6) Advice-line risk: we must ship data and diffs, never 'use classification X', with that boundary enforced in the prompt and in the UI copy.

name: Bounty Radar
one_liner: A daily-refreshed map of California Proposition 65 60-day notices, the reformulation limits buried in past settlements, and which plaintiff firms are hunting your product category right now — so consumer-product sellers see the wave before it hits them.
problem: Proposition 65 is enforced by private 'bounty hunter' plaintiffs who file 60-day notices at a rate of roughly 316-593 per month through 2025 (Jan 337, Feb 341, Mar 358, Apr 344, Jun 400, Sep 520, Oct 593) — call it 4,500-5,000 a year and rising. For an e-commerce or consumer-product seller, an attorney-negotiated settlement typically runs $10,000-$20,000, and if it does not resolve in the 60-day window and suit is filed, average settlements jump to $40,000-$90,000 before your own legal fees. The information asymmetry is total and one-directional: the plaintiff bar systematically works product categories (drinkware, vinyl bags, cookware, supplements, cosmetics) and the negotiated reformulation ppm limits that define de facto compliance live only inside settlement PDFs on the AG's site. The California AG's 60-day notice database is searchable by plaintiff, defendant, chemical, and product from 1988 to present but exposes no CSV export, no bulk download, and no API — so nobody can subscribe to 'notices against products like mine'. Sellers find out when a demand letter arrives; Amazon seller forums show them at that point asking strangers whether the letter is real and whether to call a lawyer. Free monthly PDF summaries exist (Intertek, Bureau Veritas), but they are retrospective, category-generic, and arrive weeks late.
target_customer: US consumer-product brands and 7-8 figure Amazon/Shopify sellers who ship into California — housewares, drinkware, tools, jewelry, bags, supplements, cosmetics, pet products — plus the small compliance/QA teams and sourcing agents inside them. Secondary: private-label aggregators and 3PL-adjacent brand managers with 100-5,000 SKUs.
revenue_model: Self-serve monthly SaaS: a category-and-chemical watchlist tied to the customer's product catalog, priced by number of watched categories and SKUs, with a one-time paid report as the trigger-purchase entry. Stripe Checkout, in-app plan upgrades, automatic dunning, no sales contact. Continuity is natural because the threat is continuous and dated.
pricing_hypothesis: One-time 'Category Threat Report' $199 (instant, self-serve: notice velocity, active plaintiff firms, settlement amounts, and the prevailing reformulation ppm standard for one product category). Starter $99/mo (3 categories, daily notice alerts, safe-harbor warning-text generator). Growth $249/mo (15 categories, BOM chemical watch against the OEHHA list and safe-harbor levels, competitor-defendant tracking). Brand $599/mo (catalog CSV sync, unlimited categories, ECHA SVHC + state PFAS calendar, API). Hormozi framing: the offer is 'see the notice wave 30-90 days before it reaches your SKU' priced at ~1-2% of a single $20k settlement.
knowledge_base: The moat is assembly, not access. (1) California AG 60-day notice database — scraped daily and normalized into structured rows (AG number, notice date, plaintiff, plaintiff's attorney, defendant, product/source, chemical); the AG offers no export, so a clean structured mirror with 1988-present history is a genuine cornered resource (Helmer). (2) AG settlement/judgment filings — the crown jewels: we parse the PDFs to extract per-category reformulation limits in ppm, civil penalty splits, and attorney-fee amounts, building the only structured table of 'what concentration actually settles' by product category and chemical. (3) OEHHA Prop 65 chemical list plus No Significant Risk Levels and Maximum Allowable Dose Levels, with listing effective dates (a chemical listing starts a 12-month clock before warnings are required — a dated, predictable event we can alert on). (4) CPSC recall feed. (5) ECHA REACH SVHC candidate list (updated roughly twice yearly, Jan and Jun). (6) State chemical-restriction effective-date calendar (CA, ME, MN, WA PFAS and heavy-metal rules). Refresh cron: 03:00 PT daily paginated delta scrape of the notice DB keyed on AG number; 04:00 PT Sunday settlement-PDF harvest and extraction; OEHHA list checked daily for revision date; CPSC hourly; ECHA monthly poll; state calendar monthly. Staleness detection: the notice DB is expected to gain rows every business day — three consecutive business days with zero new AG numbers trips the watchdog, halts 'threat score' rendering, and shows a dated stale-feed banner with the last confirmed notice date.
autonomy_case: A1: signup with email + Stripe; the $199 category report is bought and delivered before any account setup, and subscriptions upgrade/cancel in-app. Onboarding is picking categories from a list our own corpus generated, or dropping a catalog CSV. A2: every deliverable is generated — the threat score, the plaintiff-firm dossier, the ppm reformulation table, the daily notice digest, and the safe-harbor warning text (which is a template fill from the OEHHA chemical name and the regulation-specified format, not drafting). No human review, no queue. A3: low-confidence behavior is the core design constraint, because a false 'you're safe' is the dangerous output. When category matching is weak, the engine refuses to emit a threat score at all: it prints 'no close precedent — 4 loose matches at 0.41 similarity', shows those four notices verbatim with their AG numbers and dates, and drops the user into a raw keyword-filtered feed instead. When a settlement PDF yields no extractable ppm figure, the row is rendered 'limit not stated in settlement' with a link to the source PDF page rather than an inferred number. Every claim carries the primary-source URL and notice date (Lewis et al. 2020 RAG grounding — retrieve, cite, and abstain rather than generate). If a month produces only unresolved cards for an account, the app auto-issues a prorated credit. There is no 'talk to our expert' path and no attorney referral — the product's stated boundary is that it reports what has been filed and settled, and never advises on liability. A4: all six sources refresh on the crons above and are diffed against the prior snapshot; the daily-row expectation gives us a genuine liveness signal, not just a timestamp. A5: scrape, parse, score, send, bill, and monitor all run unattended; a parse-rate drop below threshold on the settlement extractor blocks publication of that batch rather than shipping garbage. A6: zero human minutes; support load is bounded because the two predictable questions ('what is this notice' and 'does this apply to me') are the product's own screens.
time_to_first_revenue: 4-6 weeks. Week 1-2: notice-DB scraper and normalized store with full history backfill. Week 3: public free notice search + defendant/plaintiff/category pages (this is also the entire SEO channel — people search their own company name and the phrase 'Prop 65 60-day notice' the day the letter arrives). Week 4: $199 category report checkout. Week 5-6: watchlists, daily alerts, warning-text generator, subscriptions.
risks: (1) Unauthorized-practice-of-law and advice-liability line — the product must stay strictly descriptive (what was filed, what settled, at what ppm) and never opine on exposure; this constrains copy, prompts, and the answer bot, and is a real ongoing discipline. (2) Scrape fragility and rate-limiting on oag.ca.gov; mitigation is slow polite crawling, a full local history that retains value during outages, and the stale-feed fail-closed. (3) Purchase is trigger-driven (people buy the day the letter arrives), which is great for the one-time report but hurts subscription retention; mitigation is making the daily category feed genuinely habit-forming and pricing annual. (4) California-only scope caps TAM; mitigation is the ECHA SVHC and state-PFAS layers turning it into a general restricted-substance watch. (5) Prop 65 reform legislation could suppress private enforcement volume and gut the category overnight — a genuine single-point-of-failure regulatory risk. (6) Settlement-PDF extraction quality is the moat and the weakest link; it must be measured, with a published per-field parse-confidence and abstention rather than silent errors.

name: DutyDrift
one_liner: Matches every Federal Register trade action, Commerce scope ruling, administrative-review rate, and HTS revision against the specific HTS-code-and-origin pairs an importer actually files — and prices the retroactive liability, not just the headline tariff.
problem: Small and mid importers are structurally blind to the expensive half of trade policy. The visible half — Section 232/301 rates — is now covered by free trackers and newsletters. The expensive half is antidumping/countervailing duty: an importer 'can post a zero percent AD/CVD cash deposit on an entry and still owe six figures eighteen months later, once Commerce finishes reviewing the rate', with final margins running 'from a few percent to several hundred percent of the goods' value', plus separate 19 U.S.C. 1592 penalties if CBP opens an EAPA evasion case. A zero deposit does not mean out of scope — it means the last calculated rate for that exporter happened to be zero. Most small importers check the deposit rate once, assume the question is closed, reserve nothing, and never track the administrative-review anniversary calendar. Meanwhile the general tariff surface changed constantly through 2025-26 (2026 HTS Revision 15 by August 2026; new 10% and 12.5% rates on 60 economies finalized 23 Jul 2026 effective 24 Jul 2026 — a one-day window). A 2026 competitive review of trade-alert services finds the free options unusable ('the volume is unmanageable... filtering happens entirely on your side' for the Federal Register; CSMS 'assumes reader knows which messages apply to their codes'; weekly law-firm digests 'miss changes with short effective-date windows'; generic monitors fail because 'keyword match is not catalog match') — and that same review does not address AD/CVD or scope rulings at all. The named personalized entrant is in private beta; the closest self-serve tool is free during a research preview with no AD/CVD depth.
target_customer: Importers of record doing $2M-$150M in landed value a year in AD/CVD-exposed goods — steel and aluminum derivatives, fasteners, cabinets and vanities, quartz surfaces, solar components, tires, wire and cable, mattresses, chemicals — specifically the controller, ops lead, or owner who signs the customs bond. Also licensed customs brokers who want a monitoring layer to hand clients under their own brand.
revenue_model: Self-serve monthly subscription metered by watched HTS-code x country-of-origin x exporter tuples, with a one-time uploaded-entry-data exposure report as the entry offer. Card-on-file, in-app upgrade, automated dunning. A per-seat broker tier creates a natural expansion path without any sales motion.
pricing_hypothesis: One-time 'Exposure Snapshot' $299 — upload an ACE ITRAC or 7501 CSV, get a generated PDF within minutes showing AD/CVD case coverage, deposit-versus-likely-final-rate gap, and unliquidated exposure by entry. Watch $149/mo (25 HTS x origin pairs, daily alerts). Exposure $399/mo (100 pairs, exporter-level case tracking, administrative-review calendar, retroactive liability model). Desk $899/mo (unlimited pairs, entry-file upload, API, broker seats). Anchor: a single unanticipated six-figure liquidation bill makes $899/mo a rounding error — price to the avoided loss (Ramanujam), not to the competitor's free tier.
knowledge_base: (1) Federal Register API filtered to International Trade Administration, USTR, CBP and Commerce documents — the controlling legal record for Section 301 actions, AD/CVD preliminary and final determinations, administrative-review results, and rescissions. (2) Commerce ITA scope rulings and scope-ruling applications — the corpus that decides whether your product is inside an order; we build a structured, searchable index of scope holdings by product description, which does not exist in usable form anywhere. (3) CBP CSMS messages — entry-filing instructions and effective dates. (4) USITC HTS export (2026 Revision 15 as of 4 Aug 2026; roughly 10-15 revisions a year). (5) USTR exclusion lists mapped to Chapter 99 subheadings, with expiry dates. (6) CBP AD/CVD case list with case numbers, exporter-specific rates and effective periods. (7) ITC sunset-review and injury-proceeding calendar. The proprietary layer is the join: a normalized graph of order -> case -> exporter -> rate -> effective period -> scope holdings, keyed to HTS x origin, with every historical rate retained so retroactive liability is computable rather than guessed. Refresh cron: Federal Register and CSMS polled hourly on business days; scope-ruling index nightly; HTS revision check daily with full re-diff on revision bump; USTR exclusion expiry calendar recomputed nightly; case-list weekly; a nightly recompute of every subscriber's exposure model against the new graph. Staleness detection: the Federal Register API publishes a known document count per day — a business day with zero matched documents, or an HTS fetch whose revision string is unparseable, halts alerting, marks all exposure figures 'as of <last good timestamp>', and pages the on-call cron (which is a retry, not a person).
autonomy_case: A1: email + Stripe, no brokerage login required, no demo. The $299 snapshot is a file upload and a checkout. A2: alerts, the duty-delta math, the administrative-review calendar, and the exposure PDF are all generated from the graph; nothing is reviewed by a person before it ships. A3: the dangerous case is scope ambiguity — whether a given product falls inside an order. The engine never asserts scope. When the match is contested it renders a 'contested scope' card containing the order's scope paragraph verbatim, the two nearest scope rulings with their holdings and citations, a similarity score, and the concrete next observable (the pending scope-ruling docket and its statutory deadline). It downgrades the account's exposure figure from a point estimate to a labelled range with the unresolved tuple broken out, and auto-subscribes the user to that docket so the ambiguity resolves itself when Commerce rules. Second degrade: where an exporter-specific rate cannot be matched to the customer's supplier name, it falls back to the all-others rate and labels it 'exporter unmatched — all-others rate applied, upper bound'. Third: any month whose alerts were all unresolved triggers an automatic in-app prorated credit. No human review, no 'ask our trade expert' button — the product's positioning is monitoring and evidence assembly, explicitly not customs advice or entry filing. A4: seven machine-readable federal sources on the crons above, with per-source liveness expectations. A5: ingest, join, recompute, alert, invoice, and monitor are all scheduled; a failed source blocks that source's alerts rather than silently emitting stale numbers. A6: zero human minutes; support is bounded because every alert already contains its own primary-source citation and effective date.
time_to_first_revenue: 4-6 weeks. Week 1-2: Federal Register + CSMS + HTS ingestion and the HTS x origin duty stack. Week 3: free public duty-lookup pages per HTS code and origin (the SEO surface — importers search their own codes). Week 4: $299 exposure snapshot with CSV upload. Week 5-6: AD/CVD case graph, scope-ruling index, subscriptions.
risks: (1) Policy volatility is the tailwind and the risk — if the tariff environment stabilizes, urgency drops; mitigation is that AD/CVD orders and administrative reviews run on a statutory calendar regardless of the political weather, which is why the wedge is AD/CVD and not headline tariffs. (2) A competitive field is already forming (Tariff Sentinel free in research preview, GingerControl Compliance Radar in private beta) — differentiation must be the AD/CVD graph and retroactive liability model, which that field's own 2026 comparison shows nobody covers. (3) Liability from a wrong exposure number is severe; mitigation is abstention-by-default, ranges over point estimates, verbatim source quotation, and a hard product boundary against advice or filing. (4) Customs brokers give informal versions of this away as relationship glue and could be either the channel or the competitor; the broker seat tier deliberately makes them the channel. (5) Scope-ruling text is long and heterogeneous — extraction quality is the real engineering risk and must be measured with published abstention rates. (6) Entry-data uploads are commercially sensitive; encryption, short retention, and a plain no-resale commitment are table stakes.

name: Denial Weather
one_liner: Reads every weekly Medicare coverage update and quarterly NCCI edit drop against the specific codes a practice actually bills, and puts a dollar figure and an effective date on each change before it starts denying claims.
problem: Medicare's coding and coverage rules change on a fixed, published, machine-readable schedule that almost no small practice can actually track. Local coverage documents refresh weekly (CMS ships MCD data sets every Thursday); NCCI procedure-to-procedure edits and Medically Unlikely Edits are republished quarterly, with individual edit files running to 475,091 records in the 2026 Q3 release; HCPCS Level II is quarterly; fee schedules are quarterly. When a claim hits a PTP edit, 'the Column One code is eligible for payment, but the Column Two code is denied unless a clinically appropriate NCCI PTP-associated modifier is also reported' — and an MUE denial is a coding denial, which means the practice cannot bill the patient for it either. So the loss is total and silent: the practice keeps billing the way it always has, discovers the change six weeks later in an EOB pile, and eats the rework and the write-offs. The incumbent tools (AAPC Codify and similar code-lookup subscriptions) are reference libraries: you must already know to go look. Nobody sells the inverse and personalized version — 'here are the 6 changes in this Thursday's drop that touch YOUR top 50 codes, in YOUR MAC jurisdiction, worth $41k against your last 90 days of volume, effective October 1.'
target_customer: 1-15 provider specialty practices with high code concentration and thin margins where a single edit change moves real money — physical and occupational therapy, behavioral health, dermatology, sleep, wound care, allergy/immunotherapy, independent labs and DME suppliers — plus the small third-party billing companies (5-100 client NPIs) that serve them and can resell the alerts.
revenue_model: Self-serve monthly subscription metered by number of watched HCPCS/CPT codes and NPIs, with a one-time quarterly impact report as the entry offer timed to the four annual edit drops (a natural, calendar-driven purchase trigger four times a year). Stripe self-serve, in-app tier changes, automated dunning. The billing-company tier is pure expansion revenue with no sales motion.
pricing_hypothesis: One-time 'Quarterly Impact Report' $149 (upload a code+volume CSV, get a dated PDF of what the next drop does to you). Practice $99/mo (50 watched codes, one MAC, weekly LCD deltas). Group $299/mo (500 codes, multi-MAC, 835-derived volumes, dollar-impact modeling). Billing Company $799/mo (multi-NPI, white-labelled client digests, API). Anchor to a single avoided denial cohort: for a mid-size PT practice one changed MUE across a quarter is routinely five figures, so $299/mo prices at a few percent of one avoided event.
knowledge_base: (1) CMS Medicare Coverage Database downloads — current and retired LCDs, Articles and NCDs, shipped as .MDB and CSV with a Read Me and data dictionary, 'updated weekly on Thursdays' (the 08/02/2026 snapshot released 08/06/2026), plus the MCD Coverage API for programmatic access. (2) NCCI PTP and MUE quarterly ZIP files for practitioner, outpatient-hospital and DME supplier services. (3) HCPCS Level II quarterly updates. (4) MPFS RVU files, OPPS Addendum B, CLFS and the DMEPOS fee schedule. (5) MAC jurisdiction map (which contractor covers which state and which LCDs therefore bind). (6) CMS transmittals and MLN Matters articles. The proprietary layer is the longitudinal diff: CMS publishes snapshots, not changelogs, so a maintained revision history that answers 'what changed in this document, in this edit pair, in this MUE value, and when did it take effect' is assembly work nobody sells to small practices. Refresh cron: MCD download and diff every Thursday 20:00 ET plus a daily Coverage API poll for out-of-band NCD activity; NCCI/MUE poll daily during the two weeks around each quarterly release (Jan/Apr/Jul/Oct 1) and weekly otherwise; fee-schedule files monthly with pinned quarterly jobs; MAC map annually; transmittals weekly. Staleness detection: every source file is hashed; if the MCD weekly file hash is unchanged across two consecutive Thursdays, or a quarterly NCCI file arrives with a record count more than 10% off the prior quarter, the pipeline fails closed, suppresses that source's alerts, and shows a dated staleness banner with the last verified release date.
autonomy_case: A1: signup, CSV upload, Stripe Checkout, and renewal all self-serve; the $149 impact report needs nothing but an email and a two-column CSV. A2: the change detection, the personalization against the customer's code list and volumes, the dollar math against their MAC's fee schedule, and the before/after policy diff are all generated; no coder reviews anything. A3: the honest failure mode is jurisdiction and applicability ambiguity — a code appears in a Billing and Coding Article but not the LCD, or the upload does not reveal place of service. The engine refuses to collapse that: it renders both outcomes with both dollar figures side by side ('applies only if your MAC is Noridian JE and POS is 11'), labels the item 'unresolved — 2 readings', quotes the governing paragraph verbatim with its document ID and version date, and lets the user set the disambiguating fact once in settings so it resolves permanently. It never asserts a modifier is 'clinically appropriate' — that is a clinical judgement and the product says so explicitly and links the CMS text instead. Items that stay unresolved are excluded from headline totals rather than folded in. No coder queue, no consult upsell, no 'contact us'. A4: six CMS sources, all machine-readable, on the crons above, with hash and record-count based staleness. A5: download, diff, personalize, send, bill, and monitor all scheduled; a source that fails validation blocks its own alerts rather than degrading silently. A6: zero human minutes; support is bounded because each alert carries the primary CMS document and the diff that produced it.
time_to_first_revenue: 5-7 weeks. Week 1-2: MCD weekly ingestion plus the LCD/Article diff engine. Week 3: free public 'what changed in this week's Thursday drop' digest and per-code change-history pages (the SEO and email-list surface). Week 4: NCCI/MUE quarterly ingestion. Week 5: $149 impact report with CSV upload and checkout. Week 6-7: subscriptions and weekly personalized digests. Fastest revenue comes from timing launch to the two weeks before a quarterly edit effective date.
risks: (1) CPT code descriptors are AMA-licensed intellectual property — a hard, real constraint: the product must be built on CMS-published HCPCS and code numbers plus customer-supplied code lists, and must not redistribute CPT descriptor text without a license. This shapes the UI and needs deciding before a line of code. (2) PHI risk if users upload raw claim files; the product should accept only code + volume + MAC and reject anything patient-identifying at the parser, keeping it out of HIPAA scope by design. (3) Healthcare buyers are slow and often defer to their billing company; mitigation is making the billing-company tier the primary wedge, since one billing company brings dozens of NPIs. (4) Entrenched reference incumbents (AAPC Codify, Find-A-Code) could add personalization; mitigation is Dunford positioning — we are not a code lookup, we are a change-and-impact monitor, and the moat is the longitudinal diff history CMS does not publish. (5) Dollar-impact estimates depend on customer-supplied volumes and will be wrong if the upload is wrong; the product must show its arithmetic and label every figure as an estimate derived from the user's own file. (6) Federal fee-schedule policy shifts could reshuffle sources; mitigation is source-agnostic ingestion with per-source health checks.

name: Redlist Radar
one_liner: Watches every FDA import alert red list, refusal report and warning letter daily for your named suppliers and product codes, and tells you a container will be detained before you load it — not after it is sitting at the port.
problem: FDA Detention Without Physical Examination is a paper detention: once a firm, a product, or a country-and-product-code pair lands on an import alert, 'every shipment tied to it gets hit with DWPE... and FDA skips the inspection entirely and detains the product on paper alone.' The importer usually discovers this as 'a frantic call' when customs will not release the shipment. The costs are immediate and compounding — demurrage at a few hundred dollars per container per day escalating after the first free days, so 'a modest 10-day delay at $200 per day equals $2,000 of demurrage on a single container. Across a 12-container shipment from China, that is $24,000 of unplanned cost on one sailing', before chassis, storage and lost margin. Detention notices carry a hard response deadline, often 10 working days, and failing it means automatic refusal; getting off an import alert can take 'from several months to over a year'. The triggers are knowable in advance — unapproved or non-GRAS ingredients, drug-style claims on a supplement label, or a U.S. Agent who never relayed an FDA notice, which is precisely how a facility gets added without the importer ever hearing about it. FDA publishes all of it: alerts organized by publish date, by industry and by country, each with named red-list and green-list firms; monthly import refusal reports; weekly enforcement and warning-letter feeds. But it is published as browsable legacy HTML with no subscription-by-supplier, so the importer with 30 suppliers has no way to know that one of them was added last Tuesday.
target_customer: US importers of record in FDA-regulated consumer categories — dietary supplements and bulk dietary ingredients, packaged foods and ingredients, cosmetics and personal care, and low-risk devices — importing from Asia, Latin America and the EU, typically $3M-$100M in annual import value with a QA/regulatory lead or an ops manager wearing that hat. Secondary: customs brokers and U.S. Agent service firms who want a monitoring layer for their book.
revenue_model: Self-serve monthly subscription metered by number of watched supplier entities and product-code x country pairs, with a one-time supplier screen as the trigger purchase. Stripe self-serve throughout; broker/agent tier with multiple client workspaces as the expansion path.
pricing_hypothesis: One-time 'Supplier Screen' $99 (paste or upload a supplier list, get a dated PDF: current alert status, red-list matches, refusal history by product code and country). Watch $149/mo (10 suppliers, daily alerts, pre-shipment green-light check). Ops $349/mo (50 suppliers, product-code x country refusal analytics, entity-variant matching, alert-history timeline). Broker $799/mo (unlimited suppliers, client workspaces, API). Anchor to the quantified loss: one avoided 12-container DWPE event is ~$24,000 of demurrage alone, so $349/mo is roughly 1.5% of a single avoided incident.
knowledge_base: (1) FDA Import Alerts — the full alert set organized by publish date, industry and country, with the per-alert red list and green list of named firms including manufacturer name, address, country and FEI where given (for example Import Alert 54-18 covering DWPE of dietary supplements and bulk dietary ingredients containing new dietary ingredients, 54-14 for dietary supplement GMP failures, and 54-16 for food-marketed products containing an active pharmaceutical ingredient). FDA publishes these as browsable pages, not as a feed — so a normalized, daily-diffed firm-level table with add/remove history is the hard-to-assemble asset. (2) FDA Import Refusal Reports (monthly) joined to product codes and countries. (3) openFDA enforcement/recall and warning-letter endpoints. (4) FDA registration and FSVP data. (5) USDA FSIS import re-inspection refusals. The proprietary layer is entity resolution: matching a customer's supplier — with its transliterated name variants, trade names, shared addresses and sister facilities — to FDA's own inconsistent firm strings, and retaining every historical add/remove event so 'when did this firm go on and come off' is answerable. Refresh cron: 05:00 ET daily crawl of the alerts-by-publish-date index and every changed alert page, diffed at the firm-entry level; openFDA endpoints polled daily; refusal reports monthly on release; FSIS weekly; registration data weekly. Staleness detection: the alert index carries publish dates — if the maximum publish date across all alerts has not advanced in 7 days, or if the crawl's parsed firm count for any alert swings more than 15% (a layout break), the pipeline fails closed, freezes alerting, and shows a dated 'last verified' banner rather than implying all-clear.
autonomy_case: A1: email + Stripe; the $99 supplier screen is a paste-a-list-and-pay flow with no account required beyond email; subscriptions upgrade and cancel in-app. A2: crawling, diffing, entity matching, alerting and the screen PDF are all generated; no analyst reviews a match. A3: the failure mode that matters is a fuzzy name match, and the engine never asserts one. Below the confidence threshold it emits a 'possible match — 0.78' card showing the customer's supplier record and the FDA firm record side by side with the differing fields highlighted, and offers a one-click confirm or dismiss inside the app (a user action on their own data, not an escalation to us). If the user does nothing, the tuple stays unconfirmed and is excluded from any 'clear' status. If entity resolution fails entirely, the account degrades to country + product-code monitoring and says so explicitly on the dashboard rather than showing green. Critically, the product never renders an affirmative 'you are clear' — it renders 'no matched alert entries as of <timestamp>, monitoring N of M suppliers resolved', because a false all-clear is the one output that could cause harm. No human escalation path exists; the boundary is stated plainly — we report what FDA has published, we do not file, respond to detentions, or advise on admissibility. A4: five federal sources on the crons above, with publish-date liveness and parse-count sanity checks. A5: crawl, diff, match, alert, bill and monitor all scheduled and failing closed. A6: zero human minutes; support load is bounded by the confirm/dismiss UI absorbing the only recurring question.
time_to_first_revenue: 4-6 weeks. Week 1-2: alert crawler, firm-level normalization and historical backfill. Week 3: free public pages per import alert and per country/product code (the SEO surface — importers and brokers search alert numbers and supplier names constantly). Week 4: $99 supplier screen with checkout. Week 5-6: watchlists, daily alerts, pre-shipment check, subscriptions.
risks: (1) Crawl fragility is the number-one operational risk — accessdata.fda.gov is legacy ASP-era HTML and returned HTTP 401 on one page during this research, so anti-bot behaviour and layout drift are live threats; mitigation is conservative crawl rates, per-alert parse validation, a full local history that keeps working during outages, and hard fail-closed on parse anomalies. (2) False negatives are the dangerous error (a missed red-list add), which forces the never-say-clear design above and a published, honest coverage scope — this is a product-integrity constraint, not marketing. (3) Entity resolution across transliterated foreign firm names is genuinely hard and is the make-or-break engineering problem; it must be measured with published precision/recall and default to abstention. (4) Customs brokers and U.S. Agent consultancies already hand out informal versions as relationship glue; the broker tier is designed to make them the channel rather than the competitor. (5) TAM is narrower than it looks because importers of record are concentrated in FDA-regulated categories; mitigation is adding FSIS and cosmetics (MoCRA) coverage to widen the base. (6) If FDA ever ships a real subscribe-by-firm feed, the monitoring layer commoditizes — the defensible remainder is the historical add/remove timeline and entity graph, which is why the history is retained from day one.

name: Redline
one_liner: Read-only OAuth into Google/Microsoft/Meta ad accounts; every time an ad platform publishes a dated policy change, Redline tells you exactly which of your live ads, keywords, assets and landing pages it will kill, and by which date.
problem: Ad platforms publish policy changes continuously with hard effective dates (Google alone shipped Prediction Markets on 2026-01-21, Limited Ad Serving expansion in June 2026, Local Services platform policy on 2026-07-06). Advertisers find out only when spend stops: an ad flips to Disapproved and delivery goes to zero — Google's own docs state a disapproved item 'won't be able to run until the policy violation is fixed and the ad is reviewed again', and Merchant Center disapprovals mean products 'stop showing across Google'. The rules are 100% public and dated; the mapping from rule text to *your* 4,000 ads is what nobody does. So agencies discover breakage retroactively at the daily budget check, after a weekend of dead campaigns. This is Graham's 'live in the future and build what's missing': the future (the effective date) is already published, the tooling to act on it before it lands is not.
target_customer: Performance marketing agencies and in-house PPC leads managing $25k–$500k/mo across 5–75 accounts — especially in policy-hot verticals (healthcare/supplements, finance/credit, legal, gambling/prediction markets, crypto, firearms adjacent, alcohol, political). Beachhead per Moore: agencies in regulated verticals, where one policy sweep hits every client at once and the agency eats the blame.
revenue_model: Flat monthly SaaS, self-serve card at signup, seat-less and account-tiered. Stripe Billing subscription with automated dunning; annual plan at 2 months free. Expansion is by connected-account count and monthly managed spend, both metered automatically from the API — a Ramanujam-style value metric that grows with the customer without a salesperson.
pricing_hypothesis: $79/mo Solo (3 accounts, $25k spend), $249/mo Studio (15 accounts, $150k spend), $599/mo Agency (75 accounts, $500k spend). Anchored directly against published competitor pricing: Opteo is $129 / $249 / $499 at 10 / 25 / 75 accounts and Optmyzr starts ~$208/mo — neither sells policy-change impact. Hormozi framing: the offer is 'never lose a weekend of spend to a policy update you could have read three weeks earlier', so price is trivially dominated by one prevented disapproval on a $50k/mo account.
knowledge_base: A versioned, diffed corpus of ad-platform rulebooks: (1) every support.google.com/adspolicy page including the dated 'Update to X policy (Month Year)' announcement pages, which carry explicit effective dates; (2) the Google Ads policy manual pages and restricted-category/certification requirement pages; (3) Microsoft Advertising policy pages; (4) Meta Advertising Standards and its enforcement/changelog pages; (5) Google Merchant Center Shopping ads policies and the product data specification. Refresh: sitemap + conditional-GET crawl hourly; full content hash diff at 02:00 UTC daily; on any diff, an extraction pass emits a structured PolicyDelta record {policy_id, prior_text, new_text, effective_date, affected_verticals, affected_entity_types, geos}. A weekly 06:00 UTC Sunday full re-crawl catches pages that changed without sitemap updates. Staleness detection: every source URL carries last_seen_200 and last_hash_change; if a source has not returned 200 in 72h the UI marks that policy family 'unverified since <date>' and suppresses new claims sourced from it. The moat is cumulative and hard to assemble retroactively — the diff history (who changed what, when, and how enforcement followed) cannot be backfilled once Google overwrites a page, which is Helmer's cornered-resource dynamic building quietly from day one.
autonomy_case: A1: Google/Microsoft/Meta OAuth at signup, Stripe Checkout on the same screen, first impact report generated within ~90 seconds of token grant — no demo, no call. A2: the deliverable is a generated impact report and a per-entity remediation list, produced entirely by the diff pipeline plus a retrieval-grounded matcher (Lewis et al. 2020 RAG — every claim is emitted with the exact policy paragraph and URL it came from, so the model retrieves rather than recalls). A3: confidence is a first-class output. Each flagged entity gets a score; below threshold the product does not guess — it renders 'Possible exposure, not confirmed', shows the retrieved policy text side by side with the ad text, states which fact it could not verify (e.g. 'we cannot see your landing page's disclosure block'), and narrows to the checkable claim. Zero-match runs are reported as 'no affected entities found for this delta' with the entity count scanned, never escalated. Users can dismiss a flag, which trains the account-level threshold. There is no ticket queue, no 'our team will review'. A4: crawl/diff crons above; the corpus is public HTML with no scraping-hostile auth. A5: ingestion, diff, per-account rescan (every 6h), Stripe dunning, and deploys all run on schedule; each cron has a heartbeat and fails closed — if the crawler cannot verify freshness, the account rescan is skipped and the dashboard shows the stale banner rather than emitting a stale verdict. A6: support load is bounded because the only stateful thing per customer is an OAuth token; token expiry is handled with an in-product reconnect prompt, not an email to a human.
time_to_first_revenue: 6–9 weeks to first paid self-serve subscription. Weeks 1–3: crawler + diff store over Google Ads policy pages only (single platform, deepest pain, cleanest corpus). Weeks 4–6: Google Ads API read-only entity pull + matcher + report UI + Stripe Checkout. Week 7 onward: free 'Policy Delta Digest' (public weekly diff of every ad policy change with effective dates) as the Weinberg & Mares bullseye channel — it is genuinely useful standalone, ranks for the exact policy names advertisers search after a disapproval, and converts to the paid account-mapped product.
risks: (1) Platform-risk: Google Ads API terms restrict some use cases and the app needs a developer token with basic access — mitigate by launching read-only, keeping within reporting scope, and shipping a no-OAuth 'paste your ad copy + vertical' preflight mode that needs no token at all. (2) False positives destroy trust faster than misses; mitigate with a hard precision-over-recall stance and the explicit 'unconfirmed' tier. (3) Google could ship native policy-change previews inside Ads — but they have had Policy Manager for years and still show violations only after the fact, and they will never cover Microsoft and Meta in one view. (4) Attribution problem: proving a disapproval was *prevented* is hard, so churn risk is 'nothing happened this month' — counter with the digest and a monthly 'deltas scanned / entities checked / exposures caught' receipt so the work is visible even in quiet months.

name: Sunsetter
one_liner: A read-only GitHub App that inventories every third-party platform API call in your codebase and matches it against the published deprecation and sunset calendars of Shopify, Stripe, Meta, Amazon SP-API, Google Ads and others — then opens dated issues and migration PRs before the sunset, not after the 400s.
problem: Every major platform publishes a machine-readable sunset calendar and every integrator still gets surprised. Shopify ships a new API version every quarter with only 'a minimum of 12 months' support and 'at least nine months of overlap', and the penalty is brutal and automatic: an app still calling unsupported resources 'is delisted from the Shopify App Store. Users are blocked from installing it for a minimum of seven days.' Shopify also killed legacy custom app creation after 2026-01-01. Amazon states plainly that 'calls to deprecated resources will fail beginning on their sunset date', and is removing the entire Catalog Items v0 API for sellers effective 2026-03-31. Meta expires Graph API versions on a fixed calendar. The information is all public, all dated — but nobody maps it to the 40 files in *your* repo that actually make those calls, so agencies and app vendors run a permanent low-grade panic on every quarterly release and pay engineers to re-read changelogs they have read before.
target_customer: Shopify/e-commerce app vendors and dev agencies (2–30 engineers) maintaining production integrations against 3+ platforms; also internal platform teams at DTC brands and ISVs whose revenue depends on one marketplace connector staying alive. Christensen JTBD: 'tell me what breaks, when, and where in my code, so I can put it in this sprint instead of next quarter's fire.'
revenue_model: Per-organisation SaaS via GitHub Marketplace and direct Stripe Checkout. Self-serve install, instant first scan, card required after a 14-day trial that is enforced in code. Expansion by repo count and number of platforms watched. Optional annual prepay. Renewal is fully automated through Stripe with in-product dunning banners.
pricing_hypothesis: $49/mo Solo (3 repos, 3 platforms), $199/mo Team (15 repos, all platforms, auto-PRs), $599/mo Agency (unlimited repos + client-facing exposure reports). Willingness to pay is anchored on one engineer-day: at ~$700/day fully loaded, Team pays for itself if it saves one afternoon of changelog archaeology per quarter — and the downside it prevents (Shopify App Store delisting with a 7-day install block) is existential revenue, not inconvenience. Ramanujam's rule: price against the avoided loss, not the feature list.
knowledge_base: A normalised, versioned DeprecationGraph joining two halves. Half one, platform side: Shopify GraphQL Admin SDL per version (publicly downloadable per API version) plus shopify.dev release notes and changelog.shopify.com; Stripe's public OpenAPI spec (published to GitHub, updated on every API version) plus docs.stripe.com/upgrades; Amazon SP-API deprecation schedule page plus its dated 'Deprecation Reminders' changelog entries and public SP-API OpenAPI models; Meta Graph/Marketing API changelog and version expiry table; Google Ads API release notes; Twilio, Slack, Xero, QuickBooks changelogs. Half two, customer side: an AST/regex hybrid extractor over the connected repos producing a symbol inventory (GraphQL field paths, REST endpoint paths, SDK method names, pinned API version strings in config). Refresh: nightly 03:00 UTC — pull each platform's current SDL/OpenAPI, structurally diff against the stored prior snapshot (removed fields, removed mutations, new @deprecated directives, new sunset headers), and re-scrape the changelog pages; emit DeprecationEvent {platform, symbol, deprecated_on, sunset_on, replacement_symbol, source_url}. Weekly full re-derivation on Sunday. Staleness: each platform carries last_successful_spec_pull; past 96h the platform's panel goes amber and its countdowns are labelled 'as of <date>' instead of 'live'. The defensibility is that structural schema diffs are deterministic and cheap for us and tediously expensive for each customer — and the accumulated symbol→replacement mapping table across dozens of platforms is exactly the hard-to-assemble asset the factory wants.
autonomy_case: A1: GitHub App install → repo select → scan → paywall, all in-browser; Stripe Checkout, no call. A2: output is machine-produced — an inventory table, a dated countdown, and generated pull requests for the mechanical migrations (renamed mutations, changed identifier formats, version-string bumps). No human reviews anything on our side. A3: this is the strongest low-confidence story of the five, because schema diffs are ground truth. Every claim is anchored to a concrete symbol present in a concrete spec file at a concrete version — the model does not opine on whether something is deprecated, it reads it. Where the mapping is ambiguous (the platform removed a field but published no replacement, or the call site is dynamically constructed), the product downgrades to 'Detected usage, replacement unknown' with the source_url and the exact call site, and explicitly does NOT open a PR. Generated PRs always carry a machine-checkable diff plus the spec citation, and are opened as drafts so the customer's own CI is the adjudicator — code review happens in the customer's pipeline, never in a queue we staff. A4: nightly spec pulls from public URLs; every source is a stable machine-readable artifact (SDL, OpenAPI, JSON changelog), not a fragile scrape. A5: nightly ingest, per-repo rescan on push webhook + weekly full rescan, Stripe dunning, heartbeat monitoring; a failed spec pull fails closed by freezing that platform's countdowns and surfacing the freeze rather than serving stale sunset dates. A6: zero human minutes; support is bounded to install/permission questions answered by an in-product doc.
time_to_first_revenue: 7–10 weeks. Weeks 1–3: Shopify only — SDL snapshots per version, structural differ, GraphQL field-path extractor for JS/TS and Ruby. Weeks 4–6: GitHub App, dashboard, countdown, Stripe. Week 7+: add Stripe and Amazon SP-API. Distribution via a free public 'sunset calendar' page per platform (SEO against the literal query 'is X deprecated Shopify 2026'), plus GitHub Marketplace listing, plus a free single-repo scan that returns a real count of at-risk call sites before asking for payment — Ries-style: the free scan is the experiment that measures whether the pain is real before we build the paid surface.
risks: (1) Source code access is a high-trust ask — mitigate with read-only scopes, ephemeral clones never persisted, a 'scan locally, upload only the symbol inventory' CLI mode for the paranoid, and SOC2-lite transparency page from day one. (2) Extraction coverage: dynamically constructed endpoints and heavy SDK abstraction reduce recall — mitigate by reporting measured coverage per repo ('we parsed 91% of call sites; 34 dynamic sites unresolved') rather than implying completeness. (3) Platforms may add their own in-console deprecation linting (Shopify partially does) — differentiator is cross-platform in one countdown, which no single platform will ever ship. (4) Developer-tool churn is high and $49 plans have thin margins; push toward the Team tier where auto-PRs create real switching cost.

name: Basis
one_liner: Upload a processor statement or connect Stripe, and Basis recomputes what your card processing should have cost under the currently published Visa/Mastercard/Amex interchange tables and your merchant category code — flagging misclassified MCCs, avoidable downgrades and network fees you're being billed twice for.
problem: Interchange is a public rate card that changes on a published schedule (Visa's Merchant Data Standards Manual carries an April 2026 edition; interchange schedules refresh in April and October), and merchants still have no way to check their bill against it. Two costly failure modes: MCC misclassification, where a merchant 'can operate under an incorrect code for years without a flag — silently overpaying on interchange', with acquirers not proactively auditing MCC accuracy after onboarding; and interchange downgrades, where missing Level 2/Level 3 data on commercial cards costs 50–100 basis points that submitting product codes, quantities, unit prices and tax amounts would have recovered. Industry sources put typical overpayment at 20–40% of processing cost. Today the only people who check are contingency consultants who take a cut of recovery — a model that is by construction human-judgement-heavy, slow, and adversely selected toward large merchants. Everyone under $10M in card volume is unserved. That is textbook Christensen low-end disruption.
target_customer: B2B and mixed-B2B merchants doing $500k–$20M/yr in card volume who accept commercial/purchasing cards: wholesale distributors, equipment and parts dealers, professional services, SaaS with enterprise card payers, medical/dental groups, trade suppliers. Secondary: fractional CFOs and bookkeeping firms who want a defensible monthly cost check across a client book.
revenue_model: Flat monthly subscription, explicitly NOT contingency — this is the positioning wedge (Dunford: define the alternative you are not). Self-serve signup, statement upload or Stripe OAuth, first report in minutes, Stripe Billing for renewal and dunning. Volume-banded tiers metered from the merchant's own processed volume, so the price scales with the size of the savings without renegotiation. Optional one-off $149 'single statement teardown' as a self-serve entry product that converts to subscription.
pricing_hypothesis: $99/mo under $1M annual card volume, $349/mo to $5M, $899/mo to $20M; $149 one-shot teardown. Against a cited baseline of merchants 'losing $3,000–$8,000 per month' to avoidable interchange and 50–100bp recoverable on commercial cards, a $349/mo plan on a $3M/yr merchant is ~0.14% of volume against a 0.5–1.0% opportunity — Hormozi's value equation with the dream outcome quantified, the effort near zero (upload a PDF), and the time delay measured in minutes.
knowledge_base: A parsed, versioned rate-and-rules corpus: (1) Visa USA Interchange Reimbursement Fee schedules and the Visa Merchant Data Standards Manual (the authoritative MCC list and its assignment rules, published as a dated PDF — the April 2026 edition is public); (2) Visa Core Rules and Visa Product and Service Rules, published on visa.com; (3) Mastercard US interchange programs and rates PDFs; (4) Amex OptBlue rate sheets; (5) network assessment/fee schedules (NABU, APF, FANF, Kilobyte, cross-border, and their equivalents); (6) a derived qualification matrix mapping {MCC, card product, CP/CNP, AVS/CVV presence, L2/L3 data completeness, settlement latency} → expected interchange program. Refresh: monthly 04:00 UTC on the 2nd, fetch each source PDF/HTML, hash it, and on change run a table-extraction pass into the rate store with an effective_date; hard-scheduled deep refresh on 15 April and 15 October when the networks publish. Staleness: every rate row carries source_document_version and effective_date; if the current date is past a known publication window and no new document has been ingested, the product banners 'rates last verified <date>; April 2026 schedule not yet ingested' and computes only against the dated schedule it actually holds, labelling every figure with that date. The moat is the parsed, historically versioned rate matrix — the PDFs are public but turning 60+ rate tiers across three networks into a queryable qualification matrix, and keeping the history so you can audit a statement from four months ago against the schedule in force then, is a genuinely hard-to-assemble asset.
autonomy_case: A1: signup → upload PDF/CSV statement or connect Stripe read-only → report → Stripe Checkout to unlock full detail. No call, ever. A2: parsing, matching and recomputation are entirely code — a deterministic rate engine, with the LLM used only for statement layout normalisation and for writing the plain-English explanation of each finding, both grounded in the extracted rate rows (RAG, with the rate table row and source document cited on every line item). A3: the engine reports per-transaction and per-line confidence. Where a statement's fee line cannot be mapped to a known program, it is placed in an 'Unclassified — $X, not counted toward findings' bucket and explicitly excluded from the savings total, so the headline number is always a floor, never a guess. Where the MCC question is genuinely ambiguous (a merchant whose activity spans two categories), the product shows both candidate MCCs, the manual's own assignment language, and the rate delta between them, and states 'this is a judgement call your processor makes; here is the evidence for each' — it narrows the claim rather than routing to a human. If parsing confidence for a whole statement is below threshold, the run self-voids and Stripe auto-refunds the one-off teardown fee in-product, no ticket. A4: monthly + April/October cron over public network documents. A5: ingest, parse, re-verify, billing, and monitoring all cron-driven; a failed rate ingest fails closed by refusing to compute against an unverified schedule. A6: zero human minutes; the bounded support surface is 'my statement format failed to parse', answered by a self-serve CSV template fallback.
time_to_first_revenue: 9–12 weeks — the longest of the five, because the rate-table extraction has to be right before a single dollar is charged. Weeks 1–5: ingest and parse Visa + Mastercard US schedules and the MCC manual into the qualification matrix; build the deterministic engine against hand-verified fixtures. Weeks 6–9: statement parser for the top 5 processor statement formats plus a Stripe connector, report UI, Stripe Checkout. Week 10+: launch the $149 self-serve teardown first (fastest path to a real transaction and to Fitzpatrick-style evidence that people will pay rather than just say the problem is real), then upsell monitoring. Channel: SEO against 'why did my interchange go up', 'MCC 5734 vs 7372', and the April/October rate-change news cycle, plus a free public MCC lookup and rate-delta calculator.
risks: (1) Statement format heterogeneity is the real engineering risk — hundreds of processor layouts, many as scanned PDFs; mitigate by launching with a Stripe/Adyen/Braintree API connector plus the 5 largest statement formats and hard-failing (with refund) on anything else rather than guessing. (2) Acting on findings requires the merchant to talk to their processor — we must sell the diagnosis, not the recovery, or we drift into the contingency model the gate forbids; positioning must be 'know your number' not 'we'll get it back'. (3) Network document licensing: the schedules are published but reproducing tables verbatim may draw complaints — mitigate by storing derived rate values and citing/linking rather than republishing the documents. (4) Interchange settlement litigation could change the rate landscape wholesale; that is actually a tailwind for a product whose job is tracking rate changes, but it adds ingest volatility.

name: Divisor
one_liner: A carrier rulebook simulator: feed it your shipments or just your SKU dimensions, and it re-prices them against the currently published FedEx/UPS rate cards, cubic and DIM triggers, DAS zip lists and this week's fuel table — so you see which surcharge rule change just started capturing your boxes, before the invoice arrives.
problem: Parcel pricing is a public rulebook that moves every single week, and the rule changes cost more than the headline increase. Both carriers announced a 5.9% GRI for 2026, but shippers 'will see higher all-in costs due to accessorials, cubic rules, DAS, zonal shifts and peak fees', with real increases 'often 7% to 12%'. The mechanism is rule redefinition, not rate: FedEx now uses Cubic Volume in addition to Length + Girth to determine Oversize and Additional Handling eligibility (effective Jan 2026), UPS added cubic triggers at 10,368 in³ for AH and 17,280 in³ for LPS effective 2026-01-26, and UPS started 2026 pricing on 2025-12-22, 'inserting an extra pre-holiday week at higher base rates'. Fuel surcharges change weekly and FedEx warns they are 'subject to change without notice'. A packaging change that adds half an inch can silently move a whole SKU into a surcharge band. The incumbents who solve this — Sifted, Intelligent Audit, Shipware — are enterprise, quote-form, and volume-gated ('shippers get the most value at $200,000+ in annual parcel volume'), leaving every SMB and mid-market shipper with a spreadsheet and a surprise.
target_customer: E-commerce and DTC brands shipping 500–50,000 parcels/month ($50k–$2M annual parcel spend) — below the incumbents' effective floor. Especially low-density categories (furniture, pet, home goods, sporting, apparel in poly-to-box transitions) where cubic and DIM rules bite hardest. Secondary: 3PLs who want to show clients the exposure of a packaging change.
revenue_model: Flat monthly SaaS, self-serve. Connect a carrier account (FedEx/UPS APIs both support read-only account access) or upload a shipment CSV; card at signup; Stripe Billing renewal and automated dunning. Deliberately no gain-share and no percentage of recoveries — which is both the autonomy requirement and, per Dunford, the sharpest positioning line against the audit industry. Tiers metered on monthly parcel count, pulled automatically.
pricing_hypothesis: $99/mo (to 2,000 parcels/mo), $299/mo (to 15,000), $799/mo (to 60,000 + packaging simulator + weekly delta alerts). Against a $500k annual parcel spend where the gap between the 5.9% headline and a real 7–12% is $5k–$30k/yr of unbudgeted surcharge, $299/mo is a rounding error. Ramanujam's willingness-to-pay logic: parcel spend is the second-largest COGS line for most DTC brands and the one they feel least able to see, so the value metric (parcels) is the same unit as the pain.
knowledge_base: A structured carrier rulebook store: (1) FedEx and UPS published rate and service guides — base rates by service/zone/weight, DIM divisors, cubic and length+girth trigger thresholds, accessorial definitions and amounts; (2) the weekly fuel surcharge tables, which FedEx publishes with explicit effective dates and states are 'applied weekly', keyed to the DOE on-highway diesel average and US Gulf Coast jet fuel spot price; (3) the EIA's genuinely machine-readable weekly diesel and jet fuel series (open API) so the next fuel band can be *forecast* a week ahead of the carrier's own posting; (4) DAS/EDAS and remote-area zip lists; (5) zone charts by origin zip; (6) the dated peak/demand surcharge calendars. Refresh: fuel tables + EIA series every Monday 15:00 UTC (EIA publishes Mondays); DAS/zip and zone tables monthly; full service-guide diff monthly plus a hard pull each October/November when GRIs are announced and each late December when they take effect. Every rule row carries effective_from/effective_to, so a shipment is always priced against the rulebook in force on its ship date. Staleness: if the current week's fuel table has not been ingested by Wednesday, the fuel component is labelled 'last verified <date>' and forecast figures are suppressed. The asset is the time-indexed rulebook — being able to answer 'what did the AH cubic trigger say on 14 January' three years from now is not something a shipper can reconstruct, and it compounds with every week we run.
autonomy_case: A1: signup → CSV upload or carrier OAuth → priced report → Stripe Checkout. Fully self-serve, in direct contrast to every incumbent's quote form. A2: the deliverable is a deterministic re-pricing computed by a rules engine over the versioned rulebook, plus a generated narrative of which rule changes moved which SKUs. No analyst touches it. A3: the honest limitation is contracted discounts — we usually cannot see a shipper's negotiated tariff. The product handles this in-product by being explicit about it: results default to 'published-rate basis' and every figure is labelled as such; where a shipper enters their discount schedule the engine switches to 'contract basis' and says so. When invoiced amounts and computed amounts diverge beyond tolerance and the engine cannot attribute the gap to a known rule, it reports 'unexplained variance: $X on N shipments' as its own line rather than inventing a cause. Low-confidence SKU dimension data (missing or implausible dims) is quarantined and excluded from totals with a count shown. Nothing routes to a person; the product simply narrows what it will assert. A4: weekly/monthly crons over carrier pages and the EIA API. A5: unattended ingest, weekly re-scoring of every account's SKU set against the new fuel and rule state, Stripe dunning, heartbeats; a failed rulebook pull fails closed and freezes new verdicts. A6: zero human minutes; support is bounded to CSV column mapping, handled by an in-product mapper with a downloadable template.
time_to_first_revenue: 8–11 weeks. Weeks 1–4: FedEx + UPS ground rate/DIM/cubic/AH/LPS/DAS rules encoded with effective dating, plus weekly fuel ingest and the EIA connector. Weeks 5–8: CSV ingest, SKU dimension simulator, report UI, Stripe. Week 9+: launch. The wedge product is a free public 'Will my box get hit by the new cubic rule?' calculator — enter L×W×H and weight, get an instant yes/no with the exact threshold and effective date cited. That is a perfect Weinberg & Mares bullseye asset: it ranks for the panic query, it is genuinely useful in ten seconds, and the natural next question ('how many of my SKUs?') is the paid product.
risks: (1) Rate guide ingestion is PDF-heavy and carriers restructure their documents annually — mitigate with a differ that alerts on structural change and fails closed rather than mis-parsing. (2) Without contracted rates the absolute numbers are directional; mitigate by leading with *deltas and rule-capture counts* ('412 of your SKUs newly qualify for AH') which are discount-independent and are the actual insight. (3) Carriers may restrict scraping of rate guides — mitigate by using their published APIs for rating where available and storing derived rules rather than documents. (4) Strong seasonality of attention (Oct–Jan) risks churn in spring; counter with the weekly fuel delta and packaging simulator as year-round reasons to log in. (5) Incumbents could launch a self-serve tier; their gain-share revenue model and enterprise cost base make that genuinely hard — the classic incumbent constraint.

name: Cutoff
one_liner: Connect App Store Connect and Play Console read-only, and Cutoff maps every dated app-store policy deadline onto your app's actual permissions, SDKs, data-safety declarations and target API level — so each app gets a countdown of exactly what must change and by when.
problem: Google Play publishes a structured Policy Deadlines table — a three-column list of deadline date, policy change, and resources, with eight live deadlines running from May 2026 into January 2027 — and still developers get their apps pulled. The pattern is relentless: the 15 April 2026 announcement introduced a Contacts Permissions policy and an Account Transfer policy with 'at least 30 days' to comply; the 15 July 2026 announcement extended User Data requirements to third-party AI integrations and set 31 August 2026 for the latest target API level; a further batch lands 26 August 2026 for age-restricted content and child-safety chat rules. Apple's App Store Review Guidelines change on their own cadence with dated revisions, privacy manifest and required-reason API rules attached. The consequence for missing one is removal or blocked updates. Yet the only tooling that exists is generic diff-watching — an Apify actor that diffs Apple's guidelines, a diffchecker snapshot, a diff.blog feed — none of which know anything about your app. Every studio with more than three apps is manually cross-referencing a policy table against a manifest, quarterly, forever.
target_customer: Indie developers and small studios with 3–50 live apps (hypercasual games, utilities, white-label app agencies), plus mobile leads at 20–200 person product companies who own compliance but have no compliance headcount. Beachhead: white-label and template app agencies, who ship dozens of near-identical binaries and where one policy change hits every SKU simultaneously.
revenue_model: Per-app-tiered monthly SaaS, self-serve. App Store Connect API key + Play Developer API service account are both self-issued by the customer in their own console — no sales involvement and no access to anything but metadata. Stripe Checkout at signup, automated renewal and dunning. Expansion by app count, read automatically from the connected accounts.
pricing_hypothesis: $39/mo Indie (3 apps), $149/mo Studio (15 apps), $499/mo Agency (100 apps + white-label client reports). Priced against the counterfactual: a single app removal or blocked update for a studio doing $20k/mo on one title costs more in a week than a year of the Studio plan, and the manual alternative is a senior mobile engineer spending half a day per policy batch, roughly monthly. Hormozi: high perceived likelihood of achievement (the deadlines are literally published and dated — we are not predicting, we are matching) with near-zero effort.
knowledge_base: A structured, dated policy-deadline graph joined to app facts. Policy side: (1) the Google Play Policy Deadlines table, already tabular with deadline/policy/resources columns and upcoming/past filtering; (2) every dated 'Policy announcement: <date>' page and the Play Console Announcements index; (3) the Play Developer Program Policy body text, diffed section by section; (4) the target API level requirement schedule; (5) Apple's App Store Review Guidelines with its dated revision history, plus Apple's required-reason API list and privacy manifest requirements. App side, pulled read-only: declared permissions and manifest facts, SDK/framework inventory, data-safety and privacy-nutrition declarations, target/compile SDK, IAP and subscription usage, age rating, and store metadata. Refresh: daily 05:00 UTC crawl of the deadlines table and announcement index (both are stable, well-structured URLs), full guideline body diff weekly Sunday, immediate re-match of every connected app whenever a new PolicyDeadline row or guideline delta lands. Staleness: each policy source carries last_verified; past 96h the app countdowns are stamped 'policy set as of <date>'. The compounding asset is the join table — the mapping from policy clause to observable app fact (e.g. 'Contacts Permissions policy → READ_CONTACTS in manifest without Contact Picker usage'), which is built once per policy and reused across every customer forever, and which is exactly the hard-to-assemble knowledge base the factory is looking for.
autonomy_case: A1: signup → paste App Store Connect key + Play service account JSON → per-app countdown in under two minutes → Stripe Checkout. No demo. A2: the deliverable is a generated per-app compliance countdown and remediation checklist, produced by the matcher over metadata the APIs return; nothing is hand-prepared. A3: matches are tiered by evidence strength. 'Confirmed' means a directly observable fact (target SDK 33 against a 31 August 2026 requirement — arithmetic, not judgement). 'Possible' means the policy turns on runtime behaviour we cannot observe from metadata, and the product says so explicitly: it shows the policy text, names the fact it cannot see ('we can see you declare READ_CONTACTS; we cannot see whether you use the Contact Picker'), and asks a single in-product yes/no the developer answers themselves — which is self-service, not escalation. 'Not applicable' is stated with the reason. The product never says 'contact us'; when it cannot decide, it shows the citation and the unresolved fact and lets the developer resolve it in one click. A4: daily/weekly crons over stable public Google and Apple URLs. A5: unattended ingest, re-match on every policy delta and every new app version, Stripe dunning, heartbeats; failed policy ingest freezes countdowns rather than serving stale deadlines. A6: zero human minutes; support surface is bounded to API key setup, covered by an in-product walkthrough.
time_to_first_revenue: 6–9 weeks — the fastest of the five, because the Play Policy Deadlines table is already structured and the Play Developer API returns app metadata cleanly. Weeks 1–3: ingest the deadlines table + announcement pages, build the policy→app-fact join for the ten highest-impact live deadlines, Play Developer API connector. Weeks 4–6: Apple connector, dashboard, Stripe. Week 7+: launch. Channel: a free public 'Play policy deadline calendar' with an email digest (ranks for every policy name developers search the week an announcement drops), plus a free single-app check that returns real counts before the paywall.
risks: (1) The single biggest risk is that Google already emails these announcements and shows some warnings in Play Console — the wedge must be the *join to your specific apps across both stores in one countdown*, which neither store will build for the other. (2) Metadata-only visibility caps precision on behavioural policies; mitigate with the honest three-tier evidence model rather than overclaiming. (3) Indie price points are thin and churn-prone (an indie with one app may cancel after the deadline passes) — push the Studio/Agency tiers where app count makes the manual alternative genuinely painful and where the client-facing report creates switching cost. (4) Apple's guidelines are prose, not a table, so extraction is fuzzier than Play's — mitigate by launching Play-first, where the corpus is already structured, and treating Apple as the expansion surface. (5) Both stores could restrict API metadata scopes; mitigate with a manifest/IPA-upload fallback path that needs no store connection at all.

name: Sunsetline
one_liner: Maps every third-party API, SDK, cloud service and AI model your repos actually call against a normalized database of dated vendor deprecations, and returns a hard calendar of what breaks when — with the source quote and the exact code lines affected.
problem: Vendors own the clock and you don't. Stripe retires API versions, OpenAI/Anthropic retire models, Azure and GKE retire services, Kubernetes removes APIs on a fixed release cadence. Notice arrives as one email to one person, or in an RSS feed nobody subscribes to, and teams learn about it when production breaks. Verified on HN (2026-01-11, story 'API Impact Tracker'): 'remove or change an endpoint, deploy, and a few hours later customers email saying their integrations broke.' The sources are all public and machine-readable but nobody normalizes them: Azure exposes a Release Communications RSS feed, GKE publishes per-version deprecation tables (PodSecurityPolicy deprecated 1.21 / removed 1.25; Docker node images deprecated 1.20 / removed 1.24; SHA-1 TLS certs deprecated 1.24 / removed 1.29), Kubernetes maintains a per-release removal guide (batch/v1beta1 CronJob removed in 1.25, flowcontrol v1beta3 removed in 1.32), endoflife.date exposes 464 products via free JSON. The work of joining those to your codebase is boring, recurring and nobody does it. This is Graham's 'live in the future and build what's missing' applied to a schema nobody has assembled.
target_customer: 5–50 engineer product teams with 20+ third-party integrations — fintech, marketplaces, AI-wrapper SaaS. Buyer is a staff/platform engineer or eng manager with a company card and no procurement gate (Moore: this is the early market, sold on outage-avoidance, not on category).
revenue_model: Flat monthly SaaS subscription per organisation, tiered by repo count and scan frequency. Stripe Checkout for the close, Stripe Billing for renewal and automated dunning. Annual prepay at -20%. Land on the free public radar page, expand by repo count. Pure product-led motion (Poyar/OpenView: free-to-paid self-serve with a usage-linked expansion axis).
pricing_hypothesis: Free (1 repo, weekly digest, no PRs) → $49/mo Team (10 repos, daily, Slack) → $149/mo Business (50 repos, hourly, migration PRs, webhooks, evidence export) → $399/mo Scale (unlimited + custom vendor feeds).
