Deliberately anchored above the nearest comparable (Deprecatr AI at $19/$39, which is waitlist-only and does not ship migration PRs) because we price the outcome — a prevented outage — not the crawl, per Ramanujam 'Monetizing Innovation' (design the product to the price) and Hormozi's value equation (we cut time-delay and effort, so the price moves off cost). Ellis 40% survey fires in-product at day 14 to test whether Team or Business is the real wedge.
knowledge_base: A normalized deprecation-event graph. Each event = {vendor, surface (endpoint | query param | SDK symbol | model id | managed service | k8s API group), announced_at, deprecated_at, sunset_at, replacement, source_url, source_quote, confidence}. Producers: per-vendor RSS/Atom parsers; GitHub Releases API; daily OpenAPI spec fetch-and-diff (a removed path or param is a mechanical, undeniable event); synthetic probes reading RFC 9745 Deprecation and RFC 8594 Sunset response headers; Azure Release Communications RSS (www.microsoft.com/releasecommunications/api/v2/azure/rss); GKE deprecation tables; the Kubernetes deprecated-API migration guide; endoflife.date /api/v1 (464 products, includes LLM services). Refresh crons: RSS + GitHub releases every 15 min; OpenAPI diff and HTML changelog crawl every 6 h; endoflife.date, k8s and cloud retirement pages nightly 03:00 UTC. Self-staleness: every source carries a historic median inter-event interval; at 2x that interval with no successful parse the source flips to STALE, every event derived from it is badged with its last-good date, and the customer-facing calendar shows the gap rather than pretending coverage. The moat is the per-vendor parser fleet plus the accumulated dated event history — you cannot retroactively buy 'what did Stripe's changelog say on 2026-03-14'.
autonomy_case: A1: GitHub App install → OAuth → Stripe Checkout → first scan under 5 minutes, no call. A2: the mapping is deterministic — tree-sitter parse, import/call-graph, lockfile and IaC parse; the LLM only normalizes changelog prose into the event schema and drafts migration notes, both JSON-schema-validated and rejected on failure. A3: when confidence is low the event renders as 'Unconfirmed — this language appears at <source_url> but we could not confirm it touches your code', severity is capped at INFO, it is excluded from the deadline calendar, and no PR is opened. When a source is stale the dashboard shows a dated banner and the SLA rule auto-credits the next invoice via the Stripe API. Nothing routes to a person, ever. A4: every source is public and machine-readable, on the crons above. A5: parsers run on schedules; a batch that fails schema validation is discarded and the previous good snapshot remains authoritative (fail closed rather than publish garbage); deploys, dunning and feed monitoring are all cron/webhook-driven. A6: support surface is docs plus an in-product 'why did I get this alert' panel that shows the raw source span, so the modal question answers itself; zero human minutes per customer.
time_to_first_revenue: 4–6 weeks. Ship the 25 highest-value vendors first (Stripe, Twilio, OpenAI, Anthropic, Shopify, Salesforce, AWS, Azure, GCP, GitHub, Slack, Auth0, SendGrid, Plaid, Kubernetes, Node, Python). Free public 'deprecation radar' page for those vendors is the single Bullseye channel to test first (Weinberg & Mares): it is SEO-native, links itself, and doubles as the product demo.
risks: Parser rot: vendors restructure changelogs and coverage silently degrades — mitigated by the staleness watchdog plus a generic LLM fallback parser, but it is the permanent operating cost. False positives are fatal to trust in an alerting product, hence the hard rule of never alerting without a quotable source span. Deprecatr AI is already positioned here and Renovate/Dependabot could absorb the feature. Deepest risk is urgency: nobody buys 'monitoring' until something breaks, so the product must lead with a dated calendar of already-announced deadlines the buyer is currently missing (Dunford: position against the alternative of 'we'll find out when it breaks', not against other monitors). Cloud vendors sometimes retire things with little or no notice, which caps the promise — the product must claim 'every announced deprecation', never 'no surprises'.

name: Article14
one_liner: Watches the SBOM of every version you have shipped against CISA KEV, OSV and GHSA hourly, and the moment a component you ship is confirmed actively exploited it starts the EU Cyber Resilience Act 24-hour clock and generates the ENISA early-warning and 72-hour notification drafts with the full evidence chain.
problem: From 11 September 2026 — four weeks from today — every manufacturer placing products with digital elements on the EU market must report actively exploited vulnerabilities to ENISA and the coordinating CSIRT within 24 hours, with a full notification at 72 hours. This is confirmed on the European Commission's own CRA page (entry into force 10 Dec 2024, reporting obligations 11 Sep 2026, full application 11 Dec 2027). Scope includes software shipped before the date. Penalties run to EUR 15M or 2.5% of worldwide turnover. The structural problem is that you cannot report what you cannot see: SBOM obligations are not formally enforceable until Dec 2027, which creates an implicit 15-month-early SBOM deadline — a 24-hour clock leaves no room for manual component archaeology. Small vendors have no per-release SBOM and no automated exploit watch. The incumbents are enterprise and sales-led; the one self-serve option found, sbomify, is $159/mo and is an artifact hub, not a clock.
target_customer: 10–200 person software, IoT, embedded and devtool vendors that sell into the EU and have no dedicated security team. Buyer is the CTO or head of engineering who has just been sent the CRA question by a customer or a board member. Christensen JTBD: the job is 'let me be able to answer the 24-hour clock without hiring anyone', not 'give me a vulnerability scanner'.
revenue_model: Subscription tiered by number of products and released versions under continuous watch, billed monthly via Stripe with automated dunning; annual prepay at -20%. Natural expansion axis is versions-under-watch, which grows every release, so revenue compounds with the customer's own shipping cadence without any human touch.
pricing_hypothesis: $99/mo Solo (1 product, 25 shipped versions, KEV/OSV watch, alerts) → $299/mo Team (5 products, 250 versions, ENISA 24h/72h draft generator, PagerDuty/webhook, signed immutable attestation log) → $799/mo Fleet (unlimited, customer-facing SBOM distribution portal, VEX publishing). Anchored against a EUR 15M downside and against sbomify's $159 self-serve tier. Ramanujam: willingness to pay here is driven by the deadline, not by feature count, so the packaging boundary is 'does it produce the filing artifact', which is exactly where the value step is.
knowledge_base: Three layers. (1) A per-release SBOM store: every version you ever shipped, in CycloneDX 1.6 / SPDX 3.0.1, built in your CI and stored immutably with artifact hashes — this is the asset a competitor cannot recreate for you retroactively and it is the reason the product is sticky. (2) The exploitation corpus: CISA KEV JSON feed, OSV.dev v1 API (verified live and free, returns id/aliases/affected package ranges/severity/references), GitHub GHSA, EPSS daily scores, NVD. (3) A CRA obligation model we maintain: which Art. 14 / Annex I duties attach to which event class, the 24h / 72h / 14-day decision trees, and the ENISA Single Reporting Platform field schema. Refresh crons: KEV and EPSS daily 04:00 UTC; OSV and GHSA hourly deltas; EU and ENISA guidance pages weekly with a diff alert into the obligation model's changelog. Staleness detection: if KEV has not refreshed in 36 h the product shows a red 'exploit feed stale since <timestamp>' banner and degrades to OSV-only mode with explicitly narrowed claims.
autonomy_case: A1: GitHub App plus Stripe Checkout; the first SBOM lands within one CI run, no demo. A2: SBOM generation, component matching, clock arithmetic and draft assembly are all code; the LLM writes only the narrative fields of the notification from a fixed template with the facts injected, then a validator checks every required ENISA field is present. A3: a fuzzy component-name match to a KEV entry is never clock-starting — it surfaces as 'Possible match, not clock-starting' with both records side by side and a one-click 'this is / is not my component' that writes to the customer's own VEX suppression list, narrowing future claims. The product states plainly and permanently in-product that it detects and drafts but does not file and is not legal advice. No queue, no expert, no escalation. A4: KEV, OSV, GHSA, EPSS and the EU/ENISA pages are all public and machine-readable, on the crons above. A5: CI-triggered plus scheduled; if SBOM generation fails for a release, the last good SBOM stays authoritative and the customer is told loudly that the new version is UNWATCHED — fail closed and visible, never silently green. A6: zero human minutes; the support surface is a deterministic in-product scope decision tree citing the regulation.
time_to_first_revenue: 3–5 weeks, and it is the most time-critical idea in this set. Launching in the last week of August 2026 lands directly on the 11 September 2026 obligation date. Blank's customer-development loop can run against a live deadline instead of a hypothetical, and the landing page can be a free deterministic 'are you in CRA scope' checker that captures email and converts.
risks: Scope confusion is the biggest conversion blocker — many buyers genuinely do not know if they are in scope, so the free scope checker must be deterministic and citation-backed or it becomes an advice product. Regulator guidance will move between now and Dec 2027, so the obligation model must be versioned and the guidance pages diffed weekly. Snyk, Mend and Sonatype could bundle a CRA clock and give it away; the defence is self-serve pricing and the per-release SBOM archive, not features. Compliance-theatre perception is real — the product must be honest that it is a detection and drafting engine. And the hard line: it must never claim to file on the customer's behalf, which caps the promise but keeps A2/A3 clean. HN sentiment on the CRA is politically hostile (eight stories, up to 215 points, largely about open-source burden), so messaging must be operational, not celebratory.

name: Noticeboard
one_liner: Generates the legally-correct attribution/NOTICE artifact for every release you cut, and watches your whole dependency tree for licence changes — the Redis, HashiCorp and Elastic style rug-pulls — before they land in your build.
problem: Two boring, recurring, well-specified obligations that almost nobody automates. First, everything you ship that leaves your servers owes attribution: MIT, BSD and Apache all require notice, copyleft requires more, and most small teams ship nothing or a stale hand-maintained file — until an enterprise customer's legal review asks for the attribution document and the deal stalls. Second, licences change underneath you: Redis moved from BSD-3 to RSALv2/SSPL at version 7.4 (announced March 2024, non-retroactive), Terraform moved MPL 2.0 to BSL in August 2023, Elasticsearch to SSPL in January 2021. Socket's writeup records the downstream consequence — Redis 'is being actively pinned to older versions, or just outright removed from repositories, linux distributions'. Nobody reads the LICENSE file of 1,400 transitive dependencies on a schedule. The source of truth is fully public and machine-readable: the SPDX License List is at v3.28.0 dated 2026-02-20 with per-licence JSON in the spdx/license-list-data repo, versioned and rebuilt on every release. FOSSA occupies the top of this market at $20/project/month (their own example works out to $207/mo for ten projects) with an enterprise motion above it; the SMB self-serve tier is thin and does not include a relicensing watch.
target_customer: 3–50 engineer teams shipping software that leaves their infrastructure — desktop and mobile apps, containers, on-prem installs, SDKs, firmware — plus any SaaS that has to survive enterprise legal review. Buyer is the founding engineer or eng lead who just got the attribution request in a procurement thread.
revenue_model: Subscription tiered by repo count, with the per-release attribution artifact as the unit of value. Stripe Checkout and Billing, automated dunning, annual at -20%. Expansion is repo count plus the hosted public attribution page, which becomes a link on the customer's own site and is therefore very hard to churn out of.
pricing_hypothesis: $39/mo Indie (3 repos, NOTICE per release, relicensing watch) → $119/mo Team (15 repos, CI policy gate, copyleft linkage analysis, dated archive) → $349/mo Business (unlimited repos, SPDX/CycloneDX export, self-hosted runner, customer-facing attribution page on your domain). Priced under FOSSA's effective per-project rate at the low end so the comparison is trivially favourable, then differentiated upward on the relicensing watch, which FOSSA does not sell as a product. Hormozi: the offer is 'never be the reason the deal stalls in legal', bundled with 'never be surprised by a rug-pull'.
knowledge_base: Three layers, one of which is a genuine time-moat. (1) The SPDX License List, machine-readable JSON, one file per licence and exception, versioned vX.Y.Z tracking the list release — pure ingestion. (2) The obligation matrix, which we author and maintain: per SPDX ID x distribution mode (SaaS / binary / container / statically linked / dynamically linked / modified source) which obligations trigger — attribution text, licence copy, written source offer, modification statement, patent grant, network-use trigger, notice placement. SPDX gives you the licence identity for free; nobody gives you the obligation encoding, and that is the product. (3) The relicensing event history: per package, dated snapshots of the declared licence across every published version, built by walking registry metadata and repo LICENSE file hashes. You cannot retro-acquire 'what did this package's licence say on this date' once you start late — we begin accumulating on day one and backfill from registry history. Refresh crons: SPDX release watch daily; registry metadata plus LICENSE hash for the union of all customers' dependency trees nightly 02:00 UTC; a licence-change event fires within 24 h of publication. Staleness: each registry's last successful crawl timestamp is shown in-product, and a stale registry marks its packages 'last verified <date>' rather than asserting current state.
autonomy_case: A1: GitHub App plus Stripe Checkout, first NOTICE artifact generated within minutes of install. A2: licence detection is deterministic — text hashing and template matching against the SPDX licence texts — and NOTICE assembly is templated from the obligation matrix; the LLM is used only to summarise an unrecognised licence text into the obligation schema, and its output is always displayed alongside the raw text. A3: when a licence cannot be identified with high confidence the component goes into a visible 'Unresolved — N components' bucket, is excluded from any completeness claim, and the emitted artifact carries an explicit dated caveat listing them. The product refuses to stamp a clean bill it cannot support. The in-product resolve flow lets the customer paste the licence text for exact matching — still no human of ours in the loop, and no legal advice is ever offered, only obligations with citations. A4: SPDX and the package registries are public and machine-readable, on the crons above. A5: nightly crons; a failed registry crawl leaves yesterday's snapshot standing and the UI says so — fail closed. A6: zero human minutes; the support surface is the obligation matrix itself, published and browsable.
time_to_first_revenue: 4–6 weeks. Wedge and single Bullseye channel: a free 'what should be in your NOTICE file' scanner for any public GitHub repo, which is SEO-native, shareable, and produces the exact artifact the buyer will later need for a real release. Fitzpatrick's Mom Test applies to validation here — ask what they sent the last time legal asked, not whether they would buy this.
risks: Latent pain: buyers do not feel attribution until legal asks, so the relicensing watch has to carry the urgency — the Redis and HashiCorp events are memorable and recent enough to do that work. The output must never read as legal advice; it states obligations with citations and nothing more, which is both a legal safety rule and an A3 constraint. FOSSA or Snyk could compress their SMB tier and squeeze the price. Detection has real false negatives on vendored, minified or dual-licensed code, so the Unresolved bucket must be prominent rather than hidden or the whole trust model collapses. Finally, relicensing events are rare — perhaps a handful of consequential ones a year — so the watch is insurance, and insurance churns unless the NOTICE artifact carries the day-to-day value.

name: Upgrade Atlas
one_liner: For every major-version upgrade sitting in your dependency tree, produces a per-repo impact report — which specific breaking changes touch which of your files — plus the codemod PR, instead of a version bump that just fails CI.
problem: Renovate and Dependabot bump the number and leave you to read the changelog. Verified on HN: 'you need to read the changelog to figure out if there's a breaking change, you don't trust semver'; the founder of Infield, a dependency-upgrade company, states 'Things _always_ break. Every single time we do a major upgrade, there's this long tail of things we need to fix', and names the worst class as 'changes that are missing from the changelog'; jashkenas, CoffeeScript's author, calls SemVer 'a false promise'. So teams sit on old majors, which then converts into an EOL and CVE problem three years later. The reading work is boring, mechanical, exactly specified by public artifacts (CHANGELOGs, UPGRADING guides, migration docs, and the published artifacts themselves), and completely unautomated — the tools that exist bump versions, they do not tell you what breaks in your code.
target_customer: 5–60 engineer teams on Node, Python, Ruby or Java whose lockfile has not seen a major bump in 18+ months. Buyer is the tech lead who has an upgrade on the backlog they keep deferring because they cannot scope it. Christensen JTBD: the job is 'let me estimate and then execute this upgrade', not 'keep my deps fresh'.
revenue_model: Two-sided: a monthly subscription tiered by repo count for continuous impact reports and codemod PRs, plus one-off high-ticket 'migration pack' credits for teams that want a single big jump they have been deferring. The credit line is fully automated too — a purchase triggers a pipeline, not a person — so it is high-ticket revenue without breaking A2.
pricing_hypothesis: $79/mo Team (5 repos, impact reports, 10 codemod PRs/mo) → $249/mo Business (25 repos, unlimited PRs, CI gate, private registry support) → $699/mo Scale. Plus $199 per one-off migration pack for a named major upgrade. Ramanujam's segmentation logic: the deferred-upgrade buyer has a different willingness to pay from the keep-it-fresh buyer, so sell them different things at different prices rather than averaging into one tier.
knowledge_base: Breaking-change atoms. For each (package, from_version, to_version) a normalised set of {kind: removed_symbol | renamed | signature_change | default_change | behaviour_change | config_key, symbol_path, replacement, codemod_id, source_url, source_span, confidence}. Two independent producers: (a) LLM extraction from CHANGELOG, UPGRADING, migration guides and release notes; (b) mechanical public-API surface diffs computed by downloading both published artifacts from the registry and diffing exported symbols and type signatures — TypeScript declarations, Python AST/inspect, Ruby method tables, Java class files. Atoms confirmed by both producers are HIGH confidence; changelog-only is MEDIUM; surface-diff-only is flagged 'undocumented breaking change', which is precisely the class practitioners say hurts most and which nothing on the market surfaces. Refresh crons: npm, PyPI, RubyGems and Maven release firehoses polled every 15 min for new majors across the union of tracked packages; surface-diff job runs on publish; changelog re-extraction on doc-hash change. Staleness: each package carries a last-analysed version, and a package whose latest release has not been analysed is shown as 'not yet analysed' rather than 'no breaking changes'.
autonomy_case: A1: GitHub App plus Stripe Checkout; the first impact report lands after the first lockfile parse, no call. A2: atoms, mapping and codemods are all code; PRs open automatically with the impact report in the body. A3: a low-confidence atom is reported as 'possible, unverified' and no codemod is applied for it — the PR body lists it under 'check these by hand' with the source span. If fewer than a threshold share of a package's atoms are HIGH, the product declines to open a PR at all and ships report-only, stating why. Nothing routes to a person. A4: registries and public docs, on the crons above. A5: crons plus a work queue; codemods run in a sandbox and must leave the test suite at least as green as before or the PR is not opened — fail closed by construction. A6: zero human minutes; the PR body is the support surface because it always carries its own evidence.
time_to_first_revenue: 5–8 weeks — the longest of the five, because the codemod runner and sandbox are real engineering. Mitigate with a report-only v1 that can ship in three weeks and monetise immediately: the impact report alone answers 'how big is this upgrade', which is the question blocking the work. Free tier is an impact report for one public repo, which is the Bullseye channel (SEO plus HN Show HN).
risks: The most contested space of the five: Infield and Ovvoc are already here and Renovate could absorb it, so this needs a sharp wedge — undocumented breaking changes found by mechanical surface diffing is that wedge and nobody else claims it. A codemod that produces subtly wrong code destroys trust instantly and permanently, hence never merging, always PR, always test-gated, never applying low-confidence atoms. Breadth is expensive: the corpus must start with the ~200 packages that cause 80% of the pain rather than chasing coverage. And per Thiel, the honest question is whether this is a product or a feature of Renovate — the answer has to be the atoms corpus, which takes years of accumulated analysis to reproduce, not the PR-opening mechanics, which take a weekend.

name: Terms Drift
one_liner: Watches the terms, DPAs, subprocessor lists, security pages and AI-training clauses of every vendor your product depends on, and turns each change into a dated, clause-level diff with a risk classification and a ready-to-file evidence record.
problem: GDPR Article 28(2) gives you the right to object to a new subprocessor, but the market-standard objection window is roughly 15 days (30–60 when negotiated), and EDPB Opinion 22/2024 requires the window be long enough for meaningful, informed objection. The failure mode is documented precisely: 'if a vendor gives thirty days to object and you check quarterly, the cadence has silently waived the right.' Vendor notification emails land in spam and not every vendor notifies at all, so independent checking of the authoritative page is the actual control. Separately, every technical team now depends on AI vendors whose data-retention and model-training clauses move quarterly, and SOC 2, ISO 27001 and DORA all require a dated vendor-review record. Today teams either do nothing or bolt on a generic byte-diff monitor. That substitution is measurable: PageCrawl sells exactly this generic capability self-serve at $13.33–$83.25/mo — proof of willingness to pay for scheduled page monitoring, with zero domain intelligence. It tells you bytes changed; it does not tell you a US-jurisdiction subprocessor was added and your 15-day clock started.
target_customer: The CTO or head of engineering at a 10–150 person SaaS who personally owns the DPA and answers the security questionnaire, plus agencies and MSPs managing this across several clients. Dunford: position against 'we check when we remember', not against other monitoring tools.
revenue_model: Subscription tiered by number of vendors watched and check frequency, Stripe Checkout and Billing with automated dunning, annual at -20%. Agency tier with multi-workspace is the high-ticket expansion path. Marginal cost per customer is near zero because the crawl is shared: one fetch of a vendor's subprocessor page serves every customer watching that vendor, so gross margin improves with every new customer on an already-tracked vendor.
pricing_hypothesis: $29/mo Starter (15 vendors, weekly checks, email) → $99/mo Team (75 vendors, daily, Slack, clause classification, evidence export) → $299/mo Business (300 vendors, hourly, API, multi-workspace for agencies, signed quarterly PDF evidence pack). Priced roughly 2–4x PageCrawl because the deliverable is a classified obligation event with an objection deadline, not a byte diff — Ramanujam's rule that you charge for the value metric the buyer actually cares about, which here is 'did my objection window open', not 'how many pages did you fetch'.
knowledge_base: A dated snapshot archive of roughly 5,000 vendor governance surfaces — subprocessor lists, DPAs, ToS, privacy policies, security and trust pages, status/incident histories, AI-usage and training-data clauses — normalised to text, hashed, versioned, and classified against a clause ontology: subprocessor added / removed, jurisdiction change, transfer-mechanism change, retention change, training-on-customer-data change, liability cap change, breach-notification window change, certification lapse. The archive is the moat and it is a pure time-moat: a competitor starting in 2027 cannot buy 'what did Vendor X's subprocessor list say on 2026-03-14'. It compounds and it is shared across all customers. Refresh crons: tier-1 vendors (top 500) every 6 h; tier-2 daily 01:00 UTC; tier-3 weekly Sunday 02:00 UTC; a customer-requested new vendor enters the crawl within 15 minutes. Staleness detection is the core safety property: every surface carries a last-successful-fetch timestamp displayed on the vendor card, and three consecutive failures flip the surface to UNWATCHED with a dated banner — the product never reports 'no change' when what actually happened is 'no fetch'.
autonomy_case: A1: email signup, pick vendors from a catalogue or paste URLs, Stripe Checkout — under three minutes to first watch. A2: crawl, normalise, diff, classify and notify are all code plus a schema-constrained LLM classifier, and the raw before/after text is always attached to the event. A3: when the classifier is unsure it emits 'Unclassified change' showing the diff with no risk score and asserts no obligation. When a page is behind a login or a bot wall the vendor card states 'cannot observe — vendor blocks automated access' with the date, and the product offers a one-click forwarding address so the vendor's own notice emails can be parsed instead. Every degradation resolves inside the product; there is no queue and no analyst. A4: all surfaces are public pages, on the crons above. A5: crons plus fail-closed staleness as described — silence is never rendered as safety. A6: zero human minutes; the vendor catalogue is self-service and the evidence pack generates on a schedule.
time_to_first_revenue: 3–4 weeks — the simplest build of the five and therefore the fastest to a first dollar. Single Bullseye channel: a free public 'subprocessor change feed' for the top 200 SaaS and AI vendors, which is SEO-native, earns links from compliance and engineering blogs, and is itself the product demo. Ries: this is the smallest MVP in the set that still delivers the full loop of value.
risks: The crowded end of the field: PageCrawl, DPAFlow, Registora and Orbiq are all present, and generic change-detection (including free changedetection.io) is 'good enough' for the cheapest buyer — so the whole differentiation load sits on clause classification and the evidence pack, not on the monitoring. Vendors increasingly block crawlers behind Cloudflare, which caps coverage; the honest answer is the transparent UNWATCHED state plus email-forwarding fallback, but it does limit the promise. Trust-centre vendors (Vanta, Drata) are adjacent and could bundle this. And the sharpest risk against the stated angle: the buyer may be a GRC person rather than a technical one, which would make this a different company than the factory intends — worth validating with Mom Test questions about who actually noticed the last subprocessor change before committing.

name: Bipsheet
one_liner: Upload your monthly merchant statement; get every fee line matched against the published Visa/Mastercard/Discover interchange and assessment tables, with the unmatched dollars named.
problem: Every US small business that takes cards receives a 4-12 page monthly merchant statement engineered to be unreadable, and loses money in three places it cannot see. (1) Downgrades: transactions falling into expensive interchange categories because of missing enhanced data, batch settled >24h, keyed entry, or AVS mismatch. (2) Silent markup drift: processor agreements permit rate increases with 30 days' notice delivered as one line in the statement footer. (3) Invented line items: 'network fees' that correspond to nothing in the published tables. The tables that govern all of it ARE public - the Visa USA Interchange Reimbursement Fees PDF I downloaded is 877KB and stamped '18 April 2026, Visa Public' - but no owner reads 100+ pages of MCC-by-product-by-qualification grids. The pain just got sharper: Visa's CEDP change on 24 Jan 2026 raised Level 2 small-business interchange ~75bps and Product 3 ~65bps, so merchants sending 'unverified' enhanced data now pay MORE than merchants sending none - an inversion almost no SMB has noticed. On $60k/mo volume, 40bps of undetected drift is $240/mo, $2,880/yr.
target_customer: US SMBs processing $25k-$500k/month on cards - restaurants, clinics, contractors, and especially B2B wholesalers and service firms (highest value because CEDP/Level 2-3 qualification is where the biggest swings are). Buyer is the owner or the bookkeeper, not a CFO.
revenue_model: Pure SaaS subscription, Stripe self-checkout. $39/mo Solo (1 merchant ID, monthly statement decode + effective rate + unattributed-fee bucket); $99/mo Multi (up to 5 MIDs, month-over-month drift alerts, interchange category breakdown, CEDP/Level-2 qualification report); $249/mo Portfolio (up to 25 MIDs, for franchisees and multi-location groups, CSV/API export). Annual prepay -20%. No recovery share, no switch commission, no processor referral revenue - neutrality is the product.
pricing_hypothesis: Ramanujam's rule: price against the quantified loss, not against cost. Typical identified leakage is $200-$600/mo, so $99 sits at a ~4x value ratio - inside Hormozi's no-brainer band. Entry at $39 is deliberately below the threshold where a small-business owner needs to think or ask anyone (a swipe-sized decision, which is what makes A1 self-serve actually convert). Value metric is merchant IDs (Poyar): it grows as the customer grows, so expansion is automatic. Expect ~$39 median at launch, blended ARPU drifting to ~$70 as multi-location groups land.
knowledge_base: Corpus: (i) Visa USA Interchange Reimbursement Fees, public PDF, reissued each April and October - the fetched copy is effective 18 April 2026; (ii) Mastercard US interchange programs and rates, public, same semi-annual cadence; (iii) Discover and Amex OptBlue published rate sheets; (iv) network assessment and brand-fee tables (Visa APF and acquirer credit voucher, Mastercard NABU and licence fee) in bps and per-transaction terms; (v) the ISO 18245 MCC list; (vi) processor published fee schedules and the PCI/non-compliance fee patterns harvested from published merchant agreements; (vii) THE HARD PART - a parsed-layout corpus of statement geometry and fee-code taxonomy per processor family (Fiserv/First Data, TSYS/Global, Worldpay, Elavon, Heartland, Square, Stripe, Clover, Paysafe), which is assembled once and compounds with every statement processed. Refresh: nightly cron content-hashes each published schedule URL; on change, an extraction job re-parses into an effective-dated rate table. Hard checkpoints on 15 April and 15 October fail CLOSED - if no new schedule has been ingested within 7 days of the expected publication window, the app banners 'rate tables may be stale as of <date>' and suppresses drift conclusions. Visa Business News and Mastercard announcement bulletins are polled weekly to catch interim fees introduced off-cycle (e.g. the Fallback Avoidance fee added 1 April).
autonomy_case: A1: Stripe Checkout, drag in a PDF, report renders in ~60s - no demo, no call, renewal is Stripe Billing. A2: extraction, classification and repricing are code; the LLM is confined to layout-tolerant field extraction against a strict schema, and every fee line must resolve to a citation (document, effective date, program code) into the published table or it is not asserted. A3 (low confidence, resolved IN PRODUCT): a fee code that maps to no known published program is never guessed - it lands in an explicit 'Unattributed charges' bucket showing the raw statement text, the dollar amount, and 'we could not match this to a published Visa/MC/Discover program as of <effective_date>'. If parse confidence falls below threshold on more than 10% of line items, the run is marked Partial, the exact failed pages are shown, the leakage estimate is SUPPRESSED rather than fabricated, and Stripe issues an automatic credit for that month. There is no 'contact us' path anywhere in the degrade ladder. A4: as described above, with fail-closed staleness detection tied to the known semi-annual publication calendar. A5: ingestion, deploys, Stripe dunning with smart retries, and a synthetic golden statement re-scored nightly - divergence from expected output blocks the deploy pipeline. A6: zero human minutes per customer; support is an in-product fee-code glossary generated from the same corpus, so the most common question answers itself.
time_to_first_revenue: 3-5 weeks. v1 ships three processor families plus the Visa/MC tables; the free single-statement teaser (effective rate + unattributed fees) is the acquisition wedge and the paid unlock is category-level downgrade analysis plus monthly monitoring.
risks: (1) Statement PDF diversity is the real engineering risk - mitigated by shipping three processor families first and letting the 'Unattributed' bucket degrade gracefully rather than mis-parse. (2) Processors and ISOs already give away 'free statement analysis' as switch lead-gen (Swipesum, FeeQuery, merchantstatementaudit.com); the counter is Dunford-style positioning against the biased incumbent - we take no referral money and never recommend a processor. (3) Churn after the customer acts on the finding and switches; countered by making the recurring product the drift alert, not the one-time audit - Visa changes rates twice a year and processors change them whenever they like. (4) Interchange PDFs could move behind a login; mitigated by archiving every published version permanently and by redundancy across acquirer-published summaries. (5) Regulatory shock (swipe-fee legislation) could compress the whole fee stack - but that increases statement churn, which increases the need to monitor.

name: Rateproof
one_liner: Recomputes every line of your UPS and FedEx invoice against the carriers' own published rate cards, ZIP surcharge lists and weekly fuel tables - flat monthly fee, you keep 100% of what you recover.
problem: Parcel invoices arrive weekly with thousands of lines, each a function of published inputs the shipper never verifies: base rate by zone/weight/service, DIM divisor, roughly 60 accessorials, delivery-area and pickup-area surcharge ZIP lists, and a fuel surcharge that changes EVERY MONDAY indexed to EIA diesel and jet-fuel prices with a one-week lag. The 2026 GRI was a 5.9% headline (UPS effective 22 Dec 2025, FedEx 5 Jan 2026) but accessorials rose 5.5-6.0% on top and new DIM/cubic criteria for Additional Handling and Large Package push real-world cost increases to 8-12%. Up to 5% of parcel invoices contain costly errors; fuel surcharge misapplication alone is cited at 3-5% cost per shipment; address correction is $25.50 in 2026. A shipper at $20k/mo with a 2% billing error rate loses $400/mo, and the fuel component can be several times that. The existing answer is contingency audit - LateShipment's OneAudit takes 25-35% of refunds recovered - which only touches refundable errors and leaves the larger non-refundable mispricing untouched.
target_customer: Ecommerce/DTC brands and B2B distributors shipping $5k-$150k/month with UPS and/or FedEx - deliberately below the volume where Sifted, Reveel, TransImpact and ICC bother to quote. Buyer is the founder, ops lead or controller.
revenue_model: Flat subscription by parcel volume, Stripe self-checkout: $49/mo up to 1,000 parcels/mo; $149/mo up to 5,000; $349/mo up to 20,000; $799/mo up to 100,000. Annual prepay -20%. Explicitly and loudly not contingency - 'keep 100% of what you recover' is the headline, positioned directly against the 25-35% recovery share the incumbents charge.
pricing_hypothesis: Direct substitution math the buyer can do in their head: a contingency vendor at 30% on a $600/mo recovery costs $180/mo and covers only refundable errors. $149 flat costs less, and also covers the larger bucket of non-refundable leakage (fuel mis-rate, wrong zone, DIM error, residential misclassification, duplicate lines) that contingency vendors have no incentive to find because it produces no refund to skim. Value metric is parcel volume (Poyar) - perfectly correlated with the customer's own growth and with the size of the problem. $49 entry is a card-swipe decision at 11pm, which is what makes A1 real.
knowledge_base: Corpus, all published and mostly machine-readable: (i) FedEx 2026 Standard List Rates and Retail Rates in PDF AND XLS, effective 5 Jan 2026 (verified on FedEx's own rate-changes page); (ii) FedEx Delivery Area Surcharge and Pickup Area Surcharge ZIP code lists in PDF and XLS, effective 20 Jul 2026 - the single most valuable and least-audited artifact in parcel; (iii) UPS published rate and service guides plus accessorial schedules; (iv) UPS/FedEx fuel surcharge tables - UPS changes effective Monday each week, publishes a rolling 90-day history, banded against the EIA National US Average On-Highway Diesel price (ground) and USGC kerosene-type jet fuel (air), each in defined price increments; (v) the EIA weekly price series via its free public API, used as an independent check on the carrier's own banding; (vi) published service commitment times by service and lane for guarantee eligibility; (vii) origin-ZIP zone charts. THE COMPOUNDING ASSET is the effective-dated version history of all of the above - you cannot correctly reprice a June invoice with August's fuel table, and nobody sells that time series to sub-enterprise shippers. Refresh: Monday 06:00 ET cron pulls both carriers' fuel tables and the EIA series; nightly content-hash diff on rate/DAS/PAS XLS URLs; an annual GRI window watcher (mid-September announcement, late-December/early-January effective) that raises a hard alarm if the new tables have not landed.
autonomy_case: A1: self-serve - customer downloads their own UPS Billing Data or FedEx Billing Online CSV/EDI file and drops it in (no carrier credential sharing needed), Stripe Checkout, report in minutes, Stripe Billing renewal. A2: the recompute is deterministic arithmetic against effective-dated tables. No LLM sits in the money path at all; an LLM is used only to normalize unfamiliar invoice column headers, and its output is schema-validated before use. A3 (low confidence, resolved IN PRODUCT): if a shipment's ship date falls outside every ingested tariff version, or the origin ZIP/zone cannot be resolved, or an accessorial code is unrecognised, that line is quarantined into 'Not priced - no published tariff ingested for <date>' with the specific reason, and is EXCLUDED from the savings total rather than estimated. Guarantee-eligibility is asserted only where a published commitment time exists for that service/lane/date; otherwise the line reads 'commitment not published for this lane'. Every finding carries a citation to the document and revision. If total priced coverage falls below 80% of invoice lines, the run is marked Partial and billed month is auto-credited. A4: as above, fail-closed. A5: unattended weekly ingest, staleness alarms, Stripe dunning, canary invoice re-scored nightly against golden output to gate deploys. A6: zero human minutes; findings are self-explanatory because each one shows the published number next to the billed number.
time_to_first_revenue: 4-6 weeks. A shippable v1 needs only fuel-table recompute, DIM recalculation, DAS/PAS ZIP verification and duplicate detection - that alone typically clears the subscription price, and the rest of the accessorial coverage lands incrementally.
risks: (1) Carrier billing file formats change without notice - mitigated by the customer-initiated download path (stable, and no ToS exposure from scraping) plus schema-tolerant ingestion. (2) Negotiated discounts are private, so an absolute 'expected' base rate is unknowable; solved by learning each customer's effective discount from their own invoice history and auditing CONSISTENCY - a discount that silently changes mid-contract is itself a high-value finding. (3) Shrinking money-back-guarantee coverage weakens the refund narrative, which is precisely why the positioning is tariff-compliance rather than refunds. (4) Enterprise incumbents moving down-market - Christensen's asymmetry says they won't defend a $49/mo tier that cannibalises 30% contingency revenue. (5) Concentration risk if a carrier restricts billing-data export; hedged by supporting regional carriers and DHL as the corpus matures.

name: Skimline
one_liner: Recomputes every DoorDash, Uber Eats and Grubhub payout against the commission rates those platforms publish - and puts a countdown on every dispute deadline before it expires.
problem: A restaurant's third-party delivery payout statement bundles gross sales, tiered commission, ad spend, promo cost, error charges, retroactive adjustments referencing orders from weeks earlier, marketplace-facilitator sales tax and pass-through tips into one net deposit. Error charges run 25-100% of the item price plus tax, and 100% of the order subtotal if a wrong order was handed to a Dasher. Retroactive adjustments 'reference transactions from weeks ago and are notoriously hard to trace.' Dispute windows are short and unforgiving: DoorDash 14 days, Uber Eats 30, Grubhub 30. One automated reconciliation surfaced $1,840 in unresolved error credits in its first month. Meanwhile the published commission rates are moving under operators' feet - DoorDash publishes Basic 15% / Plus 25% / Premier 30% with 6% pickup, while Uber Eats has just raised Lite from 15% to 20%, pickup from 6% to 7%, and now charges 30% on Uber One member orders. Nobody in a 40-seat restaurant is recomputing 900 orders a week against a rate card that changed last Tuesday.
target_customer: Independent restaurants and small multi-unit groups (1-10 locations) doing $10k-$120k/month in third-party delivery. Enormous, underserved, and already habituated to paying $50-200/mo for point solutions. Buyer is the owner or GM.
revenue_model: Subscription per location, Stripe self-checkout: $59/mo for 1 location (up to 3 platforms); $149/mo for 2-5 locations; $399/mo for 6-20; $899/mo for 21-60 (small franchise groups and restaurant groups). Annual prepay -20%. No share of recovered money - the customer submits their own disputes through the platform portal and keeps everything.
pricing_hypothesis: At $30k/mo of delivery volume, one point of unnoticed commission drift is $300/mo, and unclaimed error credits run in the hundreds. $59 is a ~5x value ratio and, critically, sits below the threshold where a GM must ask the owner - which is what makes true self-serve conversion possible (Hormozi: reduce perceived effort and risk, not just price). Value metric is locations, the natural expansion axis for any restaurant group, so net revenue retention comes free with the customer's own growth.
knowledge_base: Corpus: (i) each platform's published merchant pricing page, versioned and content-hash-diffed with a stored screenshot as evidence - DoorDash Basic/Plus/Premier percentages and pickup rate, Uber Eats Lite/Plus/Premium plus the 2026 increases, Grubhub plans; the CHANGE ITSELF is a paid alert, since operators otherwise find out via a smaller deposit; (ii) published error-charge policies including the 25-100% bands and the per-platform dispute windows (14/30/30 days), scraped from the platforms' own help centres; (iii) state marketplace-facilitator sales-tax rules with effective dates - which entity is the statutory remitter in each state - from state DOR guidance, because the tax line is the single most error-prone item on a payout; (iv) published promotion and ad-product mechanics and their billing timing; (v) an internal, compounding corpus of payout-report schemas per platform per report version, which is the part a competitor cannot buy. Refresh: daily cron hash-diffs every published pricing and policy page; weekly pull of state DOR marketplace-facilitator guidance; when a published rate changes, every affected customer is alerted the same day with the before/after and the effective date.
autonomy_case: A1: upload the platform's own payout CSV export (every platform provides one) or connect; Stripe Checkout; report immediately; Stripe Billing renewal. A2: per-order recompute against the published plan is deterministic; the error-charge ledger is built by joining charges to their later credits, which is set arithmetic, not judgement. A3 (low confidence, resolved IN PRODUCT): orders that cannot be matched land in an explicit 'Unreconciled' bucket showing the raw rows and the precise reason (unrecognised report version, order absent from the export), excluded from the recovery total. If a platform's published rate page cannot be verified within 7 days, the engine falls back to the customer's own trailing-90-day observed effective rate and labels every comparison 'observed baseline - published rate unverified as of <date>' rather than asserting a violation. Dispute deadlines are always shown with the source policy citation and a live countdown; the product drafts the dispute text and deep-links into the merchant portal, but the RESTAURANT clicks submit - we never act as agent and never route to a person on our side. A4/A5: daily corpus refresh, fail-closed staleness banners, unattended deploys and dunning, nightly canary payout file scored against golden output. A6: zero human minutes.
time_to_first_revenue: 3-4 weeks. v1 is statement-only: commission-rate verification, error-charge/credit ledger, and dispute-deadline countdowns need no POS integration at all. POS order matching is the expansion tier, not the MVP.
risks: (1) Platform ToS friction around automated portal access - structurally avoided: the customer exports their own data and the customer submits their own disputes; we only read files they already possess. (2) Platforms could improve their own reporting, but incentives run the other way (Thiel: opacity is the incumbent's margin). (3) High restaurant churn - countered by per-location pricing, annual prepay discount, and by the fact that the rate-change alert stays valuable in a flat month. (4) Voosh, DeliverGuard and Orderout occupy adjacent ground; differentiation is the published-rate-card corpus and the deadline clock rather than generic reconciliation dashboards. (5) A platform switching to opaque bundled pricing would blunt the recompute - hedged by the observed-baseline fallback already built into the degrade ladder.

name: Tariffgrid
one_liner: Re-bills your actual electricity usage under every rate schedule your utility has on file with the PUC, and tells you in dollars which one you should be on.
problem: A small commercial electric account is billed under a rate schedule chosen years ago and never revisited, and the utility will never proactively move a customer to a cheaper eligible schedule. Wrong rate class costs businesses 15-25% more; one documented case had a restaurant owner on GS-3 when she qualified for GS-2 for three years, roughly +$400/month. Demand ratchet clauses lock the highest recorded peak as a minimum billable demand for 6-12 months at 50-90% of that peak, so a single bad afternoon inflates twelve bills. Riders stay attached after they should drop; meter multipliers and manufacturing/agricultural tax exemptions get misapplied. Every rule governing this is in a tariff sheet filed publicly with the state PUC, written for regulators, and completely opaque to the person paying the bill. Commercial and industrial facilities are commonly estimated to overpay 5-15% for exactly these reasons.
target_customer: Small commercial electric accounts spending $500-$15,000/month - restaurants, dental and veterinary clinics, gyms, machine shops, self-storage, houses of worship, small manufacturers - plus property managers and franchise groups who hold dozens of meters under one buyer.
revenue_model: Subscription per meter, Stripe self-checkout: $29/mo for up to 3 meters; $99/mo up to 15; $299/mo up to 60 (property managers, franchise groups); $799/mo up to 250. Annual prepay -20%. Subscription rather than one-shot is justified because tariffs get re-filed, riders and fuel-adjustment factors change quarterly, the customer's load shape drifts, and growing businesses cross the kW/kWh eligibility thresholds that flip them into a different schedule.
pricing_hypothesis: $29/meter against a documented $400/month misclassification is a ~13x value ratio - Hormozi territory, and low enough to be an unconsidered purchase. The revenue actually lives in the multi-meter tiers, and property managers are the highest-leverage Bullseye channel (Weinberg & Mares) because a single buyer arrives with 40 meters and no incremental fulfilment cost. Expect $29 median at launch with blended ARPU climbing toward $120 as multi-meter accounts land.
knowledge_base: Corpus: (i) the OpenEI Utility Rate Database - a FREE public API (verified: free key, no cost) covering residential, commercial, industrial and lighting rate structures for most US utilities, with explicit demandratestructure, energyweekdayschedule and seasonal/monthly fields, collected and quality-controlled continuously by Illinois State University on behalf of DOE; (ii) state PUC tariff filings and approved rate-schedule PDFs, which are the legal authority AND the freshness oracle used to detect URDB drift; (iii) utility-published eligibility rules - the kW/kWh thresholds and 'you may not switch back for 12 months' clauses that make a recommendation actionable rather than theoretical; (iv) rider and adjustment-factor tables (fuel adjustment, purchased power, storm recovery) which move quarterly; (v) the customer's own 15-minute interval data via Green Button Download/Connect, or 12 months of bill PDFs. THE COMPOUNDING ASSET is an effective-dated tariff calculator that can actually bill an arbitrary load profile under any schedule including ratchets and TOU windows, plus a growing library of parsed bill layouts per utility. Refresh: weekly URDB API sync with per-tariff revision tracking; monthly crawl of PUC tariff-filing dockets per state; any tariff whose PUC effective date is newer than the ingested revision is marked STALE and its recommendations are suppressed until re-ingested - fail closed, never rank on an outdated sheet.
autonomy_case: A1: sign up, connect Green Button or upload 12 bills, pay by card, get the ranked comparison - no call at any point. A2: the engine re-bills the customer's real interval load under every eligible schedule including demand charges, ratchets, TOU windows and riders; this is pure computation, and the LLM is used only to extract fields from bill PDFs under a strict schema. A3 (low confidence, resolved IN PRODUCT): if interval data is unavailable, results are computed from monthly kWh and billed kW and clearly labelled 'estimated from monthly data - demand-sensitive schedules cannot be evaluated on this input'; if a tariff contains rules the engine cannot fully model (unusual ratchet language, standby or interruptible provisions), that schedule is marked 'not modelable' and EXCLUDED from the ranking rather than approximated; every recommendation carries the PUC tariff sheet citation, revision date and the specific eligibility clause, so the customer can verify the claim without asking us. Where the utility requires a form to switch schedules, the product generates the completed request for the customer to submit - we never file on their behalf and never route to a person. A4/A5: weekly and monthly crons, fail-closed staleness, unattended deploys and Stripe dunning, nightly regression of a golden load profile against expected bills. A6: zero human minutes.
time_to_first_revenue: 5-7 weeks. Beachhead strategy (Moore): model one large investor-owned utility territory to full fidelity first, sell only into that territory, then widen. Billing-error checks that need no schedule change (meter multiplier, ratchet misapplied, missing tax exemption) ship in the same v1 and carry the value on their own.
risks: (1) URDB coverage and accuracy vary by utility - mitigated by PUC-sourced verification for the top ~100 IOUs and by the hard rule that unmodelable tariffs are excluded rather than guessed. (2) In deregulated states the bill splits into regulated delivery (tariff) and competitive supply (contract); v1 targets the delivery side where misclassification lives and flags supply separately rather than pretending to price it. (3) Incumbents are enterprise data vendors (RateAcuity) and contingency utility-audit consultancies - neither can serve a $29/mo self-serve buyer, and contingency is banned for us anyway, so there is no head-on collision. (4) Switching friction at the utility could blunt realised value; countered by leading with the no-switch-required billing errors and by showing the exact eligibility clause so the customer knows the request will succeed. (5) Green Button adoption is uneven - hedged by the bill-upload path, which works everywhere.

name: Allowable
one_liner: Enter your NPI and see what every payer has publicly published as your negotiated rate for each CPT code - and get alerted the month a payer quietly changes it.
problem: An independent medical practice's contracted rates live in a fee schedule signed years ago that the practice cannot easily see, and payers amend them; the practice discovers it only when revenue sags months later. Since 2022 every payer must publish, monthly and publicly, machine-readable in-network files containing the negotiated rate for each billing code tied to specific provider NPIs and TINs - the CMS schema explicitly carries provider_groups with an npi array and a tin object (type ein or npi), alongside negotiated_rate, negotiated_type (negotiated / derived / fee schedule / percentage / per diem), billing_code_modifier and service_code, across CPT, HCPCS, DRG variants and CDT. So the answer to 'what did this payer agree to pay me for 99214?' is already public - and completely inaccessible, because the files are JSON that Cigna itself warns may be 'as large as one Terabyte' and are 'not intended to be opened on personal workstations.' The firms that solved the ingestion (Turquoise Health, Serif Health - billions of rows per month, 200+ payers, 90%+ of commercially insured lives) sell enterprise contracts with no published price. No independent practice can buy this at any price today.
target_customer: Independent medical practices with 1-10 providers - primary care, orthopedics, dermatology, behavioral health, physical therapy, imaging - plus the small billing companies and RCM shops that serve them (a natural multi-tenant reseller channel).
revenue_model: Subscription per practice TIN, Stripe self-checkout: $149/mo (up to 5 NPIs, top 100 billing codes, every payer with a published record for you); $399/mo (unlimited NPIs, full code coverage, monthly change alerts, geographic market-percentile benchmarks, % of Medicare framing); $999/mo for billing companies covering up to 25 TINs. Annual prepay -15%. Nothing contingent, nothing per-claim, no PHI required for the core product so no BAA gate on signup.
pricing_hypothesis: A single silently-amended E/M rate across a 4,000-visit year is a five-figure annual swing, so $149 is a rounding error against the loss - Ramanujam's 'price to the value of the decision, not the cost of the software.' $149 is also below the level where a practice manager needs physician-owner sign-off, which is what makes genuine self-serve conversion possible in a segment famous for sales-assisted buying. Value metric is TINs plus code coverage; the billing-company tier is the high-ticket expansion and arrives with 25 practices attached.
knowledge_base: This is the deepest moat of the five. Corpus: (i) payer MRF index/table-of-contents files, naming convention <YYYY-MM-DD>_<payer name>_index.<extension>, harvested from every major payer's public transparency page with no login required; (ii) the in-network rate files themselves, STREAMED and filtered rather than stored whole, indexed down to (payer, plan, TIN, NPI, billing_code, modifier, service_code) -> negotiated_rate with an effective month; (iii) the CMS Medicare Physician Fee Schedule plus GPCI (quarterly, public) as the benchmark denominator, so every rate is expressed as % of Medicare - the unit contracts are actually negotiated in; (iv) the NPPES NPI registry (public, weekly) to resolve practice name -> NPIs -> TIN groups so onboarding is a single autocomplete; (v) the CMSgov price-transparency-guide schema versions, tracked so parsers do not silently break on a schema bump. Refresh: monthly updates are REGULATORILY MANDATED (the Departments read 'monthly' as ~30-day periods), so a monthly cron per payer re-pulls the index, diffs last_updated_on, and re-streams only changed files. A payer whose file has not updated in >40 days is flagged stale in-product with a banner rather than silently aging. The historical series - what your rate was every month for two years - is genuinely unreconstructable by a later entrant, because payers overwrite their files rather than archive them. That is a compounding, time-locked asset (Helmer's cornered resource).
autonomy_case: A1: type a practice name, pick the NPI from NPPES autocomplete, Stripe Checkout, report renders. No PHI is touched in the core product at all, so there is no BAA negotiation, no security questionnaire, no call - the usual healthcare sales friction is designed out of the product rather than sold through. A2: ingestion, indexing, benchmarking and alerting are all code. A3 (low confidence, resolved IN PRODUCT): MRF data quality is genuinely poor - CRS has published a whole report on the technical problems - so the engine never guesses. A code with no matching record shows 'not published by this payer for your TIN as of <file date>' with a link to the source file and record location. Where negotiated_type is 'percentage' or 'derived' the row is labelled as such and NOT converted into a dollar figure. Where multiple conflicting records exist for the same tuple, all of them are shown with their plan identifiers instead of the engine picking a winner. Per-row confidence is displayed, and market-percentile benchmarks are suppressed entirely when the geographic sample is below a minimum n. An optional paid-vs-published check runs the practice's 835/ERA file entirely client-side so PHI never reaches our servers. Nothing anywhere routes to a human. A4: monthly mandated refresh with fail-closed staleness. A5: unattended streaming ingest with hard cost ceilings, schema-version regression tests gating deploys, Stripe dunning. A6: zero human minutes.
time_to_first_revenue: 8-10 weeks - the longest of the five because the ingest is real distributed-systems work. Mitigated by launching a deliberate beachhead (Moore): 5 payers x 3 metros x the top 200 CPT codes, with a free 'what does <payer> publish for your NPI on 99213?' lookup as the acquisition wedge and SEO surface.
risks: (1) MRF completeness and quality is uneven and some payers publish evasively - mitigated by the hard rule of never asserting beyond what the file says and by showing coverage gaps explicitly as a feature rather than hiding them. (2) Regulatory movement - there is an active Federal Register action on Transparency in Coverage dated 23 Dec 2025; the schema-version tracker is the hedge, and any tightening of the rules strictly helps this product while any loosening is signalled months in advance. (3) Turquoise or Serif could launch a self-serve SMB tier, but it would cannibalise enterprise contracts, which is the classic incumbent disincentive. (4) Compute and storage cost against terabyte files - controlled by streaming with NPI/TIN pre-filters, never persisting whole files, and hard per-payer cost ceilings that fail closed. (5) Practices may not act on a finding, weakening perceived value - countered by selling the monthly CHANGE ALERT as the product rather than the one-time report, since a rate amendment is an event that demands a response. (6) Longest build of the five, so it should be sequenced after a faster-revenue idea rather than first.

name: Bacondesk
one_liner: Self-serve weekly certified-payroll engine: upload your payroll CSV, get a signed WH-347 plus the state e-CPR XML, pre-checked against the live wage determination before the agency ever sees it.
problem: Every contractor and subcontractor on a federally funded or state public-works job must file a certified payroll report every week, per project, per entity. DOL-derived estimates put manual WH-347 completion at over one hour per employee per report — a 15-worker crew is 15+ hours a week on paperwork alone (~$19,500/yr at $25/hr for ONE project; multi-project contractors exceed $40,000/yr in admin labour). A single WH-347 carries ~168 discrete data points per worker. Getting it wrong is not cosmetic: incorrect WH-347s are a leading cause of contracting-officer rejection (which withholds progress payments), Davis-Bacon civil penalties run up to $28,619 per violation, plus back wages with compounding interest, three-year debarment, and False Claims Act treble damages on each false submission. WHD recovered $259M in FY2025, the highest since 2019. Meanwhile every incumbent — LCPtracker, eBacon, Points North, Foundation, eMars, Elation — is demo-and-quote with $995–$4,995 setup fees and $175–$1,200/mo, and contractors describe LCPtracker exports as 'revision hell'. The self-serve fallback is QuickBooks + Excel, which cannot match WD classifications or compute fringe per hour. Nobody sells a $99 credit-card product to the sub tier that is *forced* onto agency portals but has zero tooling.
target_customer: Open-shop and merit-shop specialty contractors and subs with 5–75 field employees on public works — electrical, mechanical, paving, striping, landscaping, painting, abatement, low-voltage. Buyer is the owner/office manager who personally does payroll Friday night. Beachhead: California public works (DIR eCPR is mandatory weekly XML upload and the largest public-works market in the US), then federal WH-347 nationally, then NY/WA/NJ/IL.
revenue_model: Monthly SaaS subscription, value-metered on active prevailing-wage projects (the variable that actually drives the work), not seats. Auto-renewing card on file, in-product upgrade when a project is added, automated dunning. Annual plan at two months free.
pricing_hypothesis: $99/mo for 1 active project, $199/mo for up to 3, $399/mo for up to 10, $699/mo unlimited. Zero setup fee — the setup fee is the wedge, since every incumbent charges $995–$4,995. Free tier: one WH-347 per month, watermark-free, to seed the funnel. Ramanujam's willingness-to-pay logic is easy here: the product replaces 15+ hours/week of clerical time and removes a payment-withholding risk, so $199/mo is under 3% of the labour it displaces — price is not the objection, trust is.
knowledge_base: (1) SAM.gov Davis-Bacon general wage determinations — full decision text, county/construction-type scope, and modification history, scraped nightly (WDs are revised on Fridays; there is no official bulk download, which is exactly why the assembled copy is an asset). (2) State prevailing-wage schedules that federal WDs do not cover: CA DIR determinations (published on the Feb 22 / Aug 22 cycle with double-asterisk predetermined increases), NY DOL Article 8/9 schedules, WA L&I, NJ, IL. (3) Agency submission schemas: CA DIR CPR XML Schema v1.3 XSD, plus LCPtracker/Elation import formats. (4) Apprenticeship layer: DAS-140/DAS-142 obligations on contracts ≥$30,000 and the 1-hour-apprentice-per-5-journeyman ratio. (5) 29 CFR Parts 1, 3, 5 and CWHSSA overtime rules pulled from the eCFR API with weekly diffs. (6) The real moat: a proprietary classification crosswalk (payroll job title → SOC → WD trade class → fringe treatment) grown from every filing the product generates and every user correction, which no incumbent has because they make the contractor pick the class manually. Refresh cron: SAM.gov WD crawl 02:00 daily; state schedule crawl weekly with content hashing; eCFR diff Mondays; XSD hash check weekly with FAIL-CLOSED — if the schema hash changes, XML generation is blocked and the account sees the diff rather than silently emitting a rejectable file.
autonomy_case: A1: card-on-file signup, project setup is a 5-field form (county, construction type, WD number or 'find it for me', funding source), first WH-347 in under 10 minutes, no call. A2: the artefact is a PDF and an XML produced entirely by deterministic code — arithmetic (gross, fringe credit, cash-in-lieu, CWHSSA overtime, deductions) is plain code, never a model; the LLM only does classification mapping and narrative on the exception report. No review queue, no turnaround time. A3: if a worker's trade cannot be mapped to a WD classification above the confidence threshold, the engine refuses to guess — it shows the top-3 candidate classifications with the verbatim WD text and rate for each, blocks that line from generation, and writes the user's choice into per-account classification memory so it never asks twice. If the WD is superseded or the county/date can't be resolved, it emits a 'DRAFT — NOT CERTIFIABLE' watermark and withholds the signature block entirely. There is no 'contact support' path in the compliance flow. Auto-credit: any week where the engine emits a certifiable file that an agency rejects for an engine-caused reason is refunded by rule, no ticket. A4: corpus refreshes on the crons above and self-reports staleness — every generated report footers the WD number, WD modification date, and corpus version; a report generated against a WD that has since been modified surfaces a dashboard flag and a one-click regenerate. A5: ingestion, XSD validation, deploys, Stripe dunning, and Friday 'your CPR is due Monday' reminders all run on schedules; any crawler that fails twice marks its slice stale and the affected states switch to read-only. A6: support load is bounded because the only human-shaped question ('which class is this guy?') is answered inside the product by the candidate picker.
time_to_first_revenue: 4–8 weeks. Federal WH-347 PDF + CA DIR eCPR XML is the minimum shippable pair and covers the majority of demand. Launch motion is engineering-as-marketing (Weinberg & Mares): a free public 'find my wage determination' lookup and a free single WH-347 generator, both of which rank for the exact queries contractors already type, with the paid product as the obvious next step when they have more than one project.
risks: (1) Agency mandate risk: many awarding bodies require submission *through* LCPtracker or Elation. Mitigation — do not compete for the portal, be the engine that produces a clean import file for it; the contractor still needs the numbers right and the incumbent portals do not compute classification or fringe. (2) Payroll ingestion variance across Gusto/QuickBooks/ADP/Paychex/Foundation exports; mitigate with a strict template plus mapped importers for the top five, and fail loudly on unmapped columns. (3) Union CBA fringe schedules are not in public WDs — scope v1 to open-shop and cash-fringe contractors and say so plainly (Dunford: pick the segment you actually win). (4) State schema churn can break XML output; the fail-closed hash check turns this from a silent-corruption risk into a visible outage. (5) The SAM.gov crawl has no official bulk API and could be rate-limited or restructured — build the crawler defensively and cache aggressively. (6) Liability perception: the contractor signs the statement of compliance, not the product; every artefact must make that explicit.

name: Starcheck
one_liner: Quarterly CMS Payroll-Based Journal submission built for one building: upload payroll and scheduling, get a spec-valid XML plus a Five-Star staffing simulation that tells you exactly how many RN hours you're short before the quarter closes.
problem: Every Medicare/Medicaid-certified skilled nursing facility (~14,800 nationally) must electronically submit direct-care staffing data — including agency and contract staff — within 45 calendar days of each fiscal quarter's end (Feb 14, May 15, Aug 14, Nov 14, 11:59pm ET), in XML at fileSpecVersion 4.10.0; CMS states files at other versions will be rejected outright on or after April 1, 2026. Missing or inaccurate submission triggers an automatic one-star staffing rating, which mechanically drags the facility's overall Five-Star score down by at least one star. In January 2025 alone, 801 facilities dropped to a one-star staffing rating; more than 5% of US nursing homes were penalised in a single quarter for incomplete or inaccurate PBJ data. Employee-ID inconsistencies across systems can poison the turnover measure for six consecutive quarters — up to 18 months of depressed rating. CMS audits demand supporting documentation within five days. The root cause is banal and mechanical: payroll is in one system, scheduling in another, agency hours on a spreadsheet, and job codes get misclassified (an LPN reported under an RN code silently distorts the staffing category). The star rating is not vanity — it gates Medicare Advantage network inclusion, hospital discharge referrals, and occupancy. Existing answers are full HCM suites (Netchex, SmartLinx, Empeon) that require replacing payroll — an enormous switch to solve a 4-times-a-year file format problem.
target_customer: Independent and small-chain SNFs, 1–15 buildings, that did not buy an all-in-one HCM. Buyer is the licensed Nursing Home Administrator or the Director of Nursing whose rating is on the line, or the regional VP of Ops at a 5-building chain. Secondary: rehab and therapy staffing agencies that have to hand facilities clean hour files.
revenue_model: Per-facility monthly subscription, self-serve card, auto-renewing; multi-building accounts auto-tier by facility count. The quarterly deadline calendar is the natural retention loop — the product is worthless to cancel in month two because the next submission is always ≤45 days out.
pricing_hypothesis: $299/facility/month, or $2,990/facility/year prepaid (two months free); tiered to $199/facility at 6+ buildings and $149 at 16+. Anchored against the downside, not against a competitor: one quarter at one star is a rating hit that persists for a quarter across every referral channel — Hormozi's value equation with a dream outcome (never a one-star surprise), high perceived likelihood (the simulation is arithmetic against published cut points), near-zero time delay (answer during the quarter, not after), and near-zero effort (two CSV uploads).
knowledge_base: (1) The CMS PBJ public use files on data.cms.gov — the complete national daily nurse-staffing panel plus non-nurse staffing, published quarterly, covering every certified facility. This is the asset: nobody's private customer base can match a full-census public panel. (2) The Five-Star Quality Rating System Technical Users' Guide, which contains the actual HPRD cut points and case-mix adjustment methodology, plus its archive so historical thresholds are known. (3) The PBJ Policy Manual and the CMS job title code table. (4) The PBJ XML XSD at fileSpecVersion 4.10.0. (5) Care Compare provider information and MDS-derived census for case-mix adjustment. (6) Derived: a per-state, per-bed-size distribution of HPRD so the product can say 'you are 0.07 RN HPRD from the 4-star cut in your state's distribution' — a claim only a full-census panel supports. Refresh cron: data.cms.gov API pull monthly (PBJ PUF quarterly, Care Compare monthly); Technical Users' Guide and XSD fetched weekly and hashed — on any hash change, XML generation is BLOCKED account-wide, the diff is shown, and the cut-point tables are marked unverified until re-parsed. Federal Register and CMS QSO memo RSS monitored daily for spec announcements.
autonomy_case: A1: card signup, upload payroll export + scheduling export + agency invoice CSV, first exception report in minutes; the CCN alone bootstraps the facility profile from public CMS data, so there is nothing to configure. A2: the deliverable is a validated XML file and a PDF exception/simulation report, both generated by code — hour aggregation, HPRD arithmetic, case-mix adjustment and XSD validation are deterministic; the model is used only for fuzzy job-title → CMS job-code mapping and employee-ID reconciliation, and both are confidence-gated. No queue, no turnaround. A3: hours whose job code cannot be classified above threshold go into a quarantined bucket, are EXCLUDED from the XML, and the report shows the star impact of both extremes ('if all 412 quarantined hours are CNA you land at 3 stars; if none, 2') so the user resolves it with full information instead of calling anyone. Duplicate-employee candidates are shown side by side with the evidence for the match; the product never silently merges. If census/case-mix data is stale, the simulator widens to a labelled range rather than asserting a point estimate. If the XSD hash changed, generation is blocked with the diff — fail closed, never emit a rejectable file. A4: the corpus refreshes on the crons above and stamps every report with the PBJ PUF quarter, Users' Guide version, and XSD version used. A5: ingestion, validation, deploys, dunning, and the deadline drip (T-45/T-14/T-3 emails keyed to the four fixed dates) all run on schedules; a failed CMS crawl marks the slice stale and disables the simulator (not the XML generator) until refreshed. A6: zero human minutes per customer; support surface is 'my payroll export looks different', answered by mapped importers and a template.
time_to_first_revenue: 6–10 weeks, and the timing is unusually legible: build against one quarter, launch 45 days before Feb 14 / May 15 / Aug 14 / Nov 14. Acquisition wedge is a free public 'what is my projected staffing star this quarter' calculator seeded with the facility's own published CMS data — you can pre-compute a projection for every one of the ~14,800 facilities from public files and let each administrator claim theirs. That is Weinberg & Mares engineering-as-marketing with a pre-built audience of exactly the right size.
risks: (1) Bundling risk: payroll/HCM vendors (SmartLinx, Netchex, Empeon, Fingercheck) already ship PBJ modules, so the product must win on the simulation — the forward-looking 'how many hours short am I' answer that a submission tool does not give. (2) Purchasing may sit at the chain level rather than the building; keep self-serve but make multi-building trivially additive so a regional VP can expand without a contract. (3) CMS spec changes (the 4.10.0 cutover proves this happens) — mitigated by fail-closed hashing, but it means a hard dependency on watching CMS. (4) Case-mix/census inputs are the weakest link in the simulation; be explicit about ranges rather than overclaiming precision. (5) Small absolute market (~14,800 facilities) caps the ceiling — but at $2,990/yr, 5% penetration is ~$2.2M ARR with no salespeople, which is the right shape for this factory. (6) Reputational: a wrong star projection is worse than none, so the confidence gating must be conservative by default.

name: Tierline
one_liner: Annual EPCRA Tier II chemical inventory reporting for single-site facilities: upload your SDSs, and it tells you whether you must report at all, then produces the state-correct submission file, fire-department copy and LEPC package.
problem: Any facility storing a hazardous chemical above threshold (10,000 lb, or 500 lb / the TPQ for extremely hazardous substances) must file a Tier II inventory by March 1 every year to the State Emergency Response Commission, the Local Emergency Planning Committee, AND the fire department with jurisdiction. Maximum civil penalty for a Tier II violation exceeds $71,500 and is inflation-indexed each January; states pile on late fees. The reason this costs money is pure fragmentation, and EPA's own state-requirements page confirms there is no consolidated database or standardised format: states variously mandate E-Plan (AL, AR, GA, TN), Tier II Manager or Hazconnect (CT, DE, IN, KY), EPA's free Tier2 Submit (CO, HI, ME, OH, VT), or bespoke portals (LA, TX, WA). Field requirements diverge — Florida demands maximum amounts in pounds not range codes, Utah requires a state ID formatted UT001234, Colorado has its own State Field tab. Fees diverge — $25/facility in Alabama and Tennessee, nothing in Montana, Washington, Utah. Consultants therefore charge $1,000–$3,000 per facility, and total Tier II cost commonly runs $1,500–$7,500 per facility per year. The one modern software player, Encamp, starts around $300 per user per month and sells to multi-site enterprises. The entire long tail — the auto body shop with a plating line, the propane dealer, the ag co-op, the ready-mix plant, the brewery, the cannabis extractor — is served by nobody and pays a consultant or files nothing and hopes.
target_customer: Single-site and 2–10 site operators with no EHS department: propane and fuel distributors, agricultural retailers and co-ops, metal finishing and plating, auto body, small chemical blenders, ready-mix and asphalt, water/wastewater contract operators, breweries and distilleries, cold storage (ammonia), data centres and hospitals with large diesel/battery installations. Buyer is a plant manager or operations owner wearing the EHS hat, who last year paid a consultant $2,000 or filed late.
revenue_model: Annual subscription per facility, charged up front, auto-renewing in November — deliberately before the March 1 deadline, so the renewal decision is made when the pain is most vivid rather than in the dead season. Between filings the subscription earns its keep with SDS library hosting, chemical-change threshold monitoring, and the retained record set regulators ask for.
