pricing_hypothesis: $149/facility/year for one site, $99/facility/year at 5+, $79 at 20+. Deliberately ~10–20x under the consultant price so the buying decision needs no comparison shopping (Hormozi: make the offer so obviously good that price stops being the conversation). Add-ons: $49 one-time SDS bulk-parse for a shoebox of PDFs; $99/yr for the 312-to-313 (TRI Form R) applicability screen. Free forever: the 'do I even have to report?' threshold screen — which is genuinely the highest-value first answer and the perfect top-of-funnel asset.
knowledge_base: (1) A 50-state Tier II requirements matrix — submission platform, accepted file format, state-specific fields, fees, deadline, state ID format rules, SERC/LEPC/fire-department routing — assembled by scraping the EPA state page and each of the 50+ SERC sites. EPA explicitly says no such consolidated machine-readable list exists, which is precisely why assembling it is a cornered resource in Helmer's sense: it is available to anyone in principle and to nobody in practice. (2) The EPA Extremely Hazardous Substances list with Threshold Planning Quantities (40 CFR 355 Appendices A/B) and CERCLA reportable quantities, pulled from eCFR. (3) OSHA HazCom hazard classification mapping. (4) The EPA Tier2 Submit file specification and E-Plan import format. (5) A growing CAS → hazard class → common trade-product index built from every SDS the product parses — over time this becomes a product catalogue that lets a propane dealer pick 'propane, 30,000 gal tank' instead of uploading anything. Refresh cron: monthly crawl of the EPA state page and every SERC page with content hashing; eCFR diff on 40 CFR 355 weekly; Federal Register monitor for the January civil-penalty inflation adjustment; a full re-verification sweep of all 50 states every December before reporting season opens.
autonomy_case: A1: card signup, no call; the first meaningful output (the applicability screen — 'you are under threshold on 4 of 5 chemicals; you must report only the diesel') is free and instant, and the paid upgrade is the file generation. A2: SDS parsing, CAS matching, TPQ threshold arithmetic, state-field formatting and file emission are all code; the model reads Sections 2/3/9/14 of an SDS and is checked against the deterministic CAS registry. The user uploads the produced file to their state portal — that boundary is what keeps fulfilment fully automated (the product's deliverable is the artefact, not portal keystrokes). A3: an unparseable SDS or unresolvable CAS goes onto a 'needs your confirmation' list showing the exact SDS text the engine read, the page it came from, and three candidate matches; the submission file will NOT generate while unresolved chemicals remain. If a state's matrix entry is stale (hash changed, re-parse failed), the product says so in plain language, prints the regulator's current URL and phone number, marks that state 'verify before filing', suppresses the auto-generated cover letter rather than printing a wrong one, and offers an in-product refund on that state. No human is ever routed to. A4: the state matrix is the product, and it refreshes itself monthly with a December full sweep; every generated package carries a matrix-version stamp and each state row shows its last-verified date in the UI. A5: crawls, eCFR diffs, penalty-index updates, deploys, dunning, and the deadline drip (Nov renewal, Jan kickoff, Feb 1 / Feb 14 / Feb 25 reminders) all run on cron; two consecutive crawl failures for a state fail closed to 'verify before filing'. A6: zero human minutes; support volume is bounded by the SDS confirmation UI absorbing the only judgement call.
time_to_first_revenue: 8–12 weeks to build, but revenue is seasonal and that is a feature, not a bug — ship by early November, take money in November–February, peak in the last two weeks of February. Beachhead five high-density states first (TX, CA, OH, PA, IL) rather than all fifty (Moore: win a beachhead completely before widening). SEO is unusually favourable because the search intent is literally 'do I have to file Tier II for propane in Texas', which the free applicability screen answers better than any consultant's blog.
risks: (1) Annual cadence means one purchase decision per year and structurally high churn; mitigate by renewing in November (pre-deadline, not post), and by making the SDS library plus chemical-change monitoring worth keeping year-round. (2) Some states require a registered portal account, so the product stops at producing the file — acceptable for A2, but it caps the 'we filed it for you' promise and must be stated honestly in marketing. (3) A 50-state crawler is real ongoing engineering and one silently-wrong state row is a reputational event; the fail-closed 'verify before filing' state is the load-bearing safety mechanism. (4) Consultants bundle Tier II with SPCC, stormwater and air permits, so the switching pitch only works for facilities whose consultant does Tier II alone. (5) Facilities that under-report today may prefer to stay invisible — the free applicability screen that says 'you don't need to file' converts poorly but builds the trust and the SEO that the paid tier rides on. (6) EPA or a state could publish a unified machine-readable matrix and erode the moat; unlikely given decades of fragmentation, but the durable asset is really the SDS/CAS product index, not the state table.

name: Adviserbook
one_liner: Self-serve annual compliance artefacts for small RIAs: a 25-minute interview produces your Rule 206(4)-7 written annual review, a redlined Part 2A brochure, a Form CRS diff and the testing evidence log — every assertion benchmarked against the SEC's own bulk Form ADV corpus.
problem: Every registered investment adviser must review its compliance policies at least annually and DOCUMENT that review in writing under Rule 206(4)-7, file an ADV annual updating amendment within 90 days of fiscal year end, deliver an updated Part 2A brochure or summary of material changes to clients within 120 days, and keep Form CRS current. The rule applies identically to a two-person shop and to a $50B manager. The market price for producing these documents is $8,000–$15,000/year for ongoing consulting and $30,000–$125,000 for an outsourced CCO; one AI-branded entrant is quoted at $8,000–$15,000 per MONTH for a $200M AUM firm. Critically, every named platform in this category — COMPLY (RIA in a Box), Smartria, RegFin — refuses to publish pricing and requires a demo call; the industry pattern is explicitly 'custom pricing, no self-service purchasing available'. So the ~12,000+ small advisers below $500M AUM have exactly two options: pay four to five figures a year, or copy last year's Word template forward and hope the examiner doesn't notice — which is precisely how firms end up with a written annual review that says nothing, cites nothing, and evidences nothing. This is a document-production problem being priced as a professional-services problem.
target_customer: Solo and 2–8 person RIAs between roughly $30M and $500M AUM — fee-only planners, breakaway advisers in year one or two, small family offices — where the owner is also the Chief Compliance Officer and personally writes (or fails to write) the annual review. Excluded by design: firms that want a human CCO; they are a different segment and should buy a consultant.
revenue_model: Flat monthly or annual SaaS subscription per firm plus a one-time first-year manual build. Self-serve card, auto-renew, no contract. Renewal is naturally sticky because year two regenerates against year one's findings and produces the year-over-year remediation trail an examiner asks for — the archive is the switching cost.
pricing_hypothesis: $149/month or $1,490/year per firm, plus $499 one-time for the first-year full compliance manual build. That is roughly 10% of the $8k–$15k consulting floor for the same deliverable, produced in 25 minutes rather than six weeks. Ramanujam's point applies directly: because every competitor hides price behind a demo, publishing a number is itself the positioning (Dunford — you are not a cheaper COMPLY, you are the category of 'compliance documents you buy with a card').
knowledge_base: (1) The SEC's own bulk Form ADV archive — monthly CSV extracts of Part 1 for every SEC-registered adviser and exempt reporting adviser, plus PDF Part 2A brochures and Part 3 Form CRS documents. ~15,000 firms of structured filings and free-text disclosure, machine-readable, official, and almost nobody has turned it into a benchmarking engine. This is what makes the product's claims specific rather than generic: 'your Item 5 fee disclosure omits a wrap-fee element that 91% of advisers in your AUM band with your custodian disclose', 'your Item 8 lacks a risk paragraph that appears in 14 of the last 15 exam-priority themes'. (2) 17 CFR Part 275 and the Advisers Act, via the eCFR API with weekly diffs. (3) SEC Division of Examinations annual priorities and Risk Alerts. (4) SEC administrative proceedings and enforcement releases, mined for the deficiency themes that actually get cited. (5) NASAA model rules and state adviser rules for the state-registered tier. (6) The Marketing Rule FAQ and staff guidance. Refresh cron: ADV bulk ingest monthly (matching the SEC's own publication cadence); eCFR Part 275 diff every Monday; RSS pull of exam priorities, risk alerts and enforcement releases daily, each run through an embedding check against the product's own asserted claims — when new guidance touches a claim the product has made in a customer's document, that customer's dashboard flags the affected section and offers a free regeneration.
autonomy_case: A1: card signup, enter your CRD number, and the product pulls your live Part 1, Part 2A and CRS from public SEC data — nothing to connect, nothing to upload, no call. The interview is resumable and takes ~25 minutes. A2: the deliverable is a set of documents generated by code plus retrieval-grounded generation (Lewis et al. RAG): every paragraph is anchored to retrieved rule text or to a quantified peer statistic from the ADV corpus, and dates/deadlines/AUM arithmetic are computed, not generated. No review queue, no consultant sign-off, no turnaround window. A3: this is the idea where the low-confidence path matters most, so the rule is absolute — the engine never invents a compliance conclusion. Where retrieval confidence falls below threshold, the item is emitted as an explicit OPEN FINDING containing the verbatim rule text, the precise question the firm must answer, and the sentence 'this product did not determine this; here is the citation and the decision you must record.' An annual review with six honest open findings and citations is a strictly better artefact than a consultant's boilerplate with none, and it resolves inside the product because the adviser is the certifying author by law. There is no 'talk to our expert' button anywhere in the app. A4: the ADV corpus refreshes monthly on the SEC's schedule; every document is stamped with the corpus version, the eCFR version and the ADV vintage used, and stale-corpus detection triggers the regeneration offer described above. A5: ingest, diffs, deploys, dunning, and the fiscal-year-end deadline drip all on cron; if the ADV bulk ingest fails twice, peer-benchmark claims are suppressed product-wide (documents still generate, minus the statistics) rather than served stale — fail closed. A6: zero human minutes per customer.
time_to_first_revenue: 6–10 weeks. The distribution channel is inside the corpus itself: the ADV bulk data contains every small adviser's name, AUM, and fiscal year end, so you can build a free public 'your ADV annual amendment is due in N days' tool that is personalised, accurate, and timed — engineering-as-marketing with a built-in deadline trigger and a pre-computed audience of every firm in the country. Ellis's 40% test should be run on advisers who have completed two annual cycles, not on first-week signups.
risks: (1) Highest liability of the five. The product must be positioned unambiguously as document generation from public sources with the adviser as the certifying author — not legal advice, not a CCO, not a filing agent. Every artefact carries that on the face of it, and the OPEN FINDING mechanism is what makes the honesty structural rather than cosmetic. (2) Segment mismatch: many advisers genuinely want a person to blame, and will not buy software at any price; the answer is to not chase them. (3) Form ADV or the annual review rule could change materially, invalidating templates — the weekly eCFR diff plus corpus stamping is the defence. (4) Peer-benchmark claims must be statistically honest; overclaiming from ADV free text is the fastest way to lose credibility with a compliance audience, so suppress rather than stretch. (5) Growth churn: a firm that crosses ~$500M hires a real CCO and leaves — acceptable, and the archive still makes the exit expensive. (6) Incumbents could add self-serve pricing overnight; the durable asset is the ADV benchmarking engine, not the document templates.

name: Trustline
one_liner: Monthly three-way trust account reconciliation for brokers who hold client money: upload the bank file and the ledger export, get a dated, signature-ready worksheet plus a rolling three-year audit binder in the format your state commission actually asks for.
problem: Real estate brokers and property managers holding client funds must reconcile, monthly, three balances that have to agree — the trust account bank statement, the brokerage's internal trust ledger, and the sum of every individual client sub-ledger — and retain a signed, dated worksheet. Arizona statute (A.R.S. §32-2151) mandates the monthly three-way reconciliation and treats failure to perform it as a violation, sitting alongside commingling (with a narrow carve-out for up to $5,000 of broker funds to maintain the account) and failure to keep separate ledgers per property. South Dakota makes failure to reconcile bank, trust ledger and check register at least monthly a direct statutory violation under SDCL 36-21A-80. Oregon requires monthly reconciliation of each clients' trust account and each security deposit account, with commingling grounds for discipline regardless of intent. California's DRE publishes a standing catalogue of common violations found in audits; Colorado runs a dedicated broker financial audit programme. Reconciliation deficiencies — missing worksheets, unsigned worksheets, unexplained variances — are among the most-cited findings in state audits and a leading cause of licence discipline. And the tool most small brokerages actually use for this is Excel. The designated broker's personal licence is the collateral.
target_customer: Independent brokerages and small property-management companies — roughly 25 to 750 units under management, or a sales brokerage holding earnest money — operating in states with strict monthly reconciliation and active audit programmes (AZ, CO, NC, SD, OR, CA, TX, FL, WA). Buyer is the designated/qualifying broker personally, or the office manager doing it for them. Multi-state operators are the best segment because the rules differ per state and a spreadsheet cannot hold that.
revenue_model: Monthly SaaS per trust account, self-serve card, auto-renewing. The cadence is monthly and mandatory, so the retention loop is the strongest of the five: the product emails 'your November reconciliation is ready to sign' on the third business day of every month, forever.
pricing_hypothesis: $79/month for one trust account, $199/month for up to five, $399/month for up to fifteen (multi-state operators). Annual at two months free. Value framing is the licence, not the labour: a single disciplinary action — legal fees, consent order, remediation — costs more than a decade of subscription, and the reconciliation worksheet is the single most-cited item examiners open with. Free tier: a two-way bank-to-ledger match, clearly labelled as NOT satisfying a three-way requirement, which is honest and converts by demonstrating exactly what is missing.
knowledge_base: (1) A 50-state trust/escrow account rules matrix — reconciliation frequency, retention period, permitted broker funds in the account (e.g. Arizona's $5,000 ceiling), interest handling and removal deadlines, deposit timing, required worksheet elements, signature and dating requirements, separate-ledger-per-property rules — assembled by scraping each state real estate commission's rules, forms and guidance pages. This matrix does not exist anywhere as a machine-readable resource; it is the whole moat. (2) State commission audit checklists and examiner workpaper templates, which are published and tell you literally what the auditor will look for. (3) Published disciplinary orders from state commissions — largely public and often machine-readable — mined into a live 'what actually gets cited' ranking, so the exception report orders findings by real-world enforcement frequency rather than by the engine's guess at severity. (4) Ledger export schemas for AppFolio, Buildium, Rent Manager, Propertyware and QuickBooks. (5) OFX/CSV/BAI2 bank statement parsers. Refresh cron: monthly crawl of every state commission's rules/forms/guidance pages with content hashing; monthly ingest of new disciplinary orders to keep the citation ranking current; quarterly full re-verification of the rules matrix. A state whose rules page changed and cannot be auto-reconciled is marked 'rules updated — review before signing' and the worksheet's state-citation footer is SUPPRESSED rather than printed wrong.
autonomy_case: A1: card signup, pick your state, upload two files, first worksheet in under ten minutes; no call, no implementation. A2: three-way matching, ageing of outstanding items, negative sub-ledger detection (the number-one commingling red flag), shortage/overage computation against the state's tolerance and cure window, and worksheet rendering are all deterministic accounting code — this is the least model-dependent of the five ideas, which is exactly why it is the safest. The model is used only for fuzzy transaction description matching, and it never force-matches. A3: unmatched bank items are never silently reconciled. They are listed as exceptions with candidate matches and confidence scores, and the worksheet will not print a clean 'reconciled' attestation while a material variance is unexplained — it prints 'reconciled with N exceptions, variance $X' and requires the broker to type an explanation for each, which then becomes part of the retained record (which is what the examiner wants anyway). If the ledger export lacks sub-ledger detail, the product names the exact missing column and produces a two-way reconciliation explicitly stamped as not satisfying a three-way requirement. If the state rules row is stale, citations are suppressed and the regulator's current page is linked. Every degradation resolves on-screen. A4: the state matrix and disciplinary corpus refresh monthly on cron with content hashing and last-verified dates shown per state in the UI. A5: ingestion, crawls, deploys, dunning, the day-3 monthly reminder, and the day-20 'unsigned worksheet' nag all run on schedules; two consecutive crawl failures for a state fail closed to citation-suppressed mode. A6: zero human minutes per customer; the exception-explanation UI absorbs the only judgement in the process.
time_to_first_revenue: 4–8 weeks — the fastest of the five, because the engine is deterministic accounting plus a rules table rather than a heavy model, and monthly cadence means the retention loop starts in week one rather than a quarter or a year later. Beachhead: Arizona and Colorado first (explicit statutory monthly three-way language and an active, publicised audit programme), then NC, OR, SD, then CA/TX/FL. Acquisition: a free public 'what your state's trust account audit checklist actually asks for' page per state, generated from the assembled matrix — fifty pages of content that nobody else can produce and that ranks for the exact query a broker types the week they get an audit letter.
risks: (1) Bundling: AppFolio, Buildium and Rent Manager include reconciliation modules, so the positioning must be the AUDIT ARTEFACT layer and multi-account/multi-state coverage, not the accounting system — you sit downstream of their ledger, you do not replace it. (2) Bank statement parsing variance is the main engineering tax; mitigate with OFX/BAI2 preference, mapped importers for the top five ledgers, and a strict CSV template with loud failure on unmapped columns. (3) Many brokerages already pay a bookkeeper who 'handles it' — the wedge is that the bookkeeper produces a spreadsheet, not a state-formatted signed worksheet with an exception schedule and a retained binder. (4) State trust rules are genuinely fiddly and printing a wrong citation on a signed worksheet is the reputational failure mode; citation suppression on stale rows is the load-bearing safety mechanism. (5) Small per-account price means volume is required — offset by the multi-account tiers and by property managers who run separate operating, security-deposit and owner-draw accounts, which multiplies accounts per customer. (6) The broker signs the worksheet, not the product; that boundary must be explicit on every artefact.

name: DutyLens
one_liner: Upload your product catalog and get every SKU's 10-digit HTS code with the CBP rulings that back it, the full stacked duty rate, and an alert the moment a Federal Register action changes it.
problem: Since 29 Aug 2025 every commercial shipment into the US needs a formal entry with a 10-digit HTS code and full duty payment regardless of value or origin; CBP moved the de minimis suspension into permanent regulation on 24 June 2026 with statutory repeal following 1 July 2027. Hundreds of thousands of small sellers who never touched customs now owe 'reasonable care' on classification, while the rate stack (MFN + 301 + 232 + successor authorities) changes constantly — the Federal Register API returned tariff documents published the day before this check. The three sources that resolve this (HTS schedule, 220k+ CROSS binding rulings, Federal Register actions) are all free and all effectively unusable by a non-expert.
target_customer: US importers doing roughly $100k-$20M/yr with no in-house trade-compliance person: Shopify/Amazon/Etsy private-label sellers, small DTC brands, small manufacturers importing from Asia. They buy software on a company card without procurement.
revenue_model: Self-serve monthly SaaS tiered by SKUs under active monitoring. Signup, catalog upload, classification and ongoing rate-change monitoring all happen without contact. Stripe subscription with automated dunning and auto-renewal; cancel in-app.
pricing_hypothesis: $49/mo up to 50 SKUs, $149/mo up to 300, $399/mo up to 2,000 plus API. First 5 SKUs classified free as the acquisition hook. Anchored against $150-300 per-entry customs broker fees and against the fact that one misclassified high-volume SKU costs more than a year of subscription.
knowledge_base: Three public machine-readable corpora on independent cron schedules, all verified live during this screen. (1) USITC HTS REST export — hts.usitc.gov/reststop/exportList returns the schedule as JSON with htsno, indent, description, general/special/other rates, units, footnotes and additionalDuties per line; pulled nightly and version-diffed. (2) CBP CROSS via rulings.cbp.gov/api/search, which returns JSON ruling objects with rulingNumber, subject, tariffs, rulingDate, commodityGrouping and — critically — revokedBy/revokes/modifiedBy/modifies, so precedent staleness is a field in the data rather than a guess (a single 'backpack' query returned totalHits 1,406). CROSS is a public-domain data.gov dataset. (3) The Federal Register API (federalregister.gov/api/v1/documents.json), which returned 10,000 tariff-matching documents with the newest published 2026-08-12 — this is the rate-change trigger. Staleness is self-detecting: each corpus stores fetch timestamp and content hash; if HTS has not refreshed in 48h or CROSS in 7 days the app banners 'rates as of <date>, unverified' and suppresses new classification assertions rather than serving stale ones.
autonomy_case: A1: Shopify App Store listing plus direct web signup, card on file, CSV catalog upload, results in minutes — no call anywhere in the path to the first dollar or the renewal. A2: classification is a retrieval-and-rank pipeline over HTS + CROSS with the duty stack computed deterministically from the rate tables; no human reviews any output. A3 (when unsure): the engine returns a ranked candidate set with per-candidate CROSS citations and a calibrated confidence. Below threshold it refuses to name a single code — it shows the two or three live candidates, the duty spread between them, the rulings that separate them, and marks the SKU 'unresolved, do not file on this alone'. It never routes to a broker queue or a person; it states plainly that this SKU is one a human should price and leaves the decision with the user. If more than 20% of an uploaded catalog lands unresolved, the month is auto-refunded in-product. A4: all three sources are free, government-published, machine-readable and refresh on their own cadence, with hash/timestamp staleness gates. A5: nightly ingest, weekly full reindex, and known-answer canary SKUs run after every corpus refresh — a failed canary blocks promotion of the new index and freezes alerting rather than emitting wrong rates. A6: support is a docs site plus an in-app 'why this code' evidence trace; the only unbounded surface is billing, which Stripe's customer portal handles.
time_to_first_revenue: 2-4 weeks. All three corpora are fetchable today with no API key or registration. Distribution is the Shopify App Store plus FBA/ecommerce communities where the de minimis change is still an active margin crisis; the free 'classify 5 SKUs' tier converts at the paywall with no outbound needed.
risks: Most crowded idea in the pool: Gaia Dynamics, 3CE, Zonos Classify and the hclassify Shopify app already sell AI HTS classification, several fully self-serve. Classification errors carry genuine customer liability (the ongoing FCA customs-enforcement trend), so the A3 refusal threshold must be tuned conservatively — which directly reduces perceived value ('it wouldn't answer'). The HTS reststop and CROSS search endpoints are undocumented public JSON rather than contracted APIs and can change shape without notice, so ingestion must fail closed. Tariff churn is also the moat: if the rate landscape stabilises, the alerting half of the value decays.

name: WageLens
one_liner: Type a county, a craft and a construction type and get the legally current Davis-Bacon rate straight from the government's own record, then generate the week's WH-347 from your timesheet export.
problem: Every contractor and subcontractor on federally funded construction over $2,000 must pay the correct prevailing wage per craft per county and file a weekly WH-347 certified payroll with a signed compliance statement. Misclassification is the most common violation and carries back wages, civil penalties and debarment up to three years; a 2023 DOL rule pushed liability for subcontractors' certified payroll onto primes. The authoritative data lives on SAM.gov as 4,236 currently-active determinations, revised continuously — and mid-project revisions are the specific liability trap. Existing certified-payroll suites are quote-gated and bundle full payroll processing a small sub does not want.
target_customer: Specialty subcontractors (electrical, plumbing, concrete, HVAC, painting) with 5-50 field employees taking 2-10 public-works jobs a year, and specifically the one office person who does certified payroll alongside AP/AR and the phones.
revenue_model: Self-serve monthly SaaS priced per active certified-payroll project, auto-pausing when a project closes so the bill tracks the value metric. Card at signup, Stripe dunning, no contract, cancel in-app.
pricing_hypothesis: $79/mo for one active project, $199/mo up to five, $399/mo unlimited plus a GC roll-up view. Free unlimited rate lookups as the hook; the WH-347 generator and mid-project change alerts are the paywall. Undercuts incumbents' quote-gated $175-$2,000/mo.
knowledge_base: SAM.gov's wage-determination search index, verified live: GET sam.gov/api/prod/sgs/v1/search/?index=dbra returns Davis-Bacon determinations as JSON — 4,236 currently active — with revisionNumber, modifiedDate, publishDate, isActive, isStandard, constructionTypes (Building/Heavy/Highway/Residential) and location.state.counties on every record; sibling indexes carry SCA and CBA determinations (index=wd returned 10,122 records). This gives staleness detection for free: a nightly crawl compares revisionNumber and isActive per WD, and any project pinned to a WD whose revision increments fires a mid-project change alert to that customer — which is precisely the liability event the product exists to catch. Layered on top: the WH-347 form spec and the SF-1444 conformance procedure text from DOL, both stable public documents re-fetched monthly with a hash check.
autonomy_case: A1: web signup, card, upload or connect a timesheet CSV, first WH-347 PDF inside one session. A2: the rate lookup is a database query and the WH-347 is deterministic form population (hours x the WD rate for that craft/county/construction type, with fringe handling) — nothing is authored by judgement and nothing is reviewed by a person. A3 (when unsure): the honest failure mode is a worker whose duties match no listed classification. The product refuses to guess a rate — it shows the closest listed classifications with their rates, states that the WD does not cover these duties, and describes the DOL conformance (SF-1444) path the contractor must run with the awarding agency, explicitly saying we do not and will not file it. Every rate carries its WD number, revision and modifiedDate so an auditor can trace it. If SAM.gov is unreachable at generation time the product blocks the report rather than emitting one against a possibly-stale rate. A4: government-published JSON with revision metadata, nightly diffed, as above. A5: nightly SAM crawl, per-WD revision diff, cron-fired change alerts, and a hard failure if the index returns materially fewer records than the last successful run (guards against silent truncation). A6: the workflow is upload, generate, download; support load is bounded to CSV column mapping, handled by a template picker for the common payroll exports.
time_to_first_revenue: 3-5 weeks. Certified payroll is due weekly, so any sub on a live public job has a hard forcing function every Friday. Free county-x-craft rate lookup pages are strong long-tail SEO against essentially no structured competition, and SAM.gov/USASpending award feeds identify subs who just won DBA-covered work — a self-generating cold list that needs no human qualification.
risks: SAM.gov's sgs search endpoint is an internal API, not a documented contract — it can change shape or rate-limit, and a fallback scrape of the WD detail pages is mandatory; the fail-closed design means an outage means no reports that day. State prevailing-wage schedules, a real part of the market, are not machine-readable the way federal DBA is, so v1 must honestly scope to federal work only, which shrinks the addressable base. The market is narrower than it looks: only subs actually doing DBA-covered jobs, and many are handed a certified-payroll portal by their GC as a condition of the contract.

name: PatchRadar
one_liner: Before you run WordPress updates across your client sites, PatchRadar tells you which ones will break, why, and in what order to apply the rest.
problem: Agencies on care plans manage 20-150 client sites each running 10-30 plugins, a theme and a PHP version. Codeable's own pricing guide draws the line between $30-50/mo plans ('automated updates with no staging environment, zero development time') and its $240-$1,000+/mo plans where 'plugin updates are tested on a staging environment before they touch your live site' — the entire premium in this market is paid for update safety, and it is currently bought as human hours. Meanwhile almost every fact needed to predict breakage is already published as JSON and nobody is joining it across a portfolio.
target_customer: WordPress maintenance agencies and solo freelancers running 10-150 sites on care retainers — the ManageWP / MainWP / WP Umbrella installed base, reachable in the Advanced WordPress group, r/Wordpress and WP agency Slack/Discords.
revenue_model: Self-serve monthly SaaS priced per portfolio, not per site. A free companion plugin or a MainWP/ManageWP API key reports installed plugin/theme/PHP/WP versions; the product returns a pre-update risk report and a safe apply order. Stripe subscription, card at signup.
pricing_hypothesis: $49/mo up to 25 sites, $149/mo up to 100, $299/mo unlimited. Priced per-portfolio deliberately against WP Remote's $19.99/site/mo sandbox tier — at 40 sites that is $800/mo versus $149 — and against a single unbilled breakage-repair incident inside a $240/mo care plan.
knowledge_base: The WordPress.org plugins API, verified live: api.wordpress.org/plugins/info/1.2/ returns per-plugin JSON with version, requires (min WP), tested (max WP tested), requires_php, last_updated, active_installs, the full changelog section and a complete versions history with download links. Crawled nightly across the plugin and theme corpus, this yields deterministic, citable constraints — 'this plugin requires PHP 7.4 and this site runs 7.3', 'your theme has not been tested past WP 6.4 while this update targets 7.0.4', 'last_updated is 26 months ago, this plugin is effectively abandoned'. Second corpus: vulnerability feeds joined by slug and version (WPScan's vulnerability database API, ~21,000 entries updated daily, free tier available; plus the open WPVulnerability API). Third: changelog text diffing between the installed and target versions to extract breaking-change language and removed hooks, cross-referenced against the other plugins installed on that same site. Staleness is explicit: every report carries 'plugin index as of <timestamp>', and if the WP.org crawl is more than 36h stale the report degrades to constraints-only and suppresses the softer conflict layer entirely.
autonomy_case: A1: install a free plugin or paste a MainWP API key, see the report immediately, upgrade in-app on a card. A2: the constraint engine is pure computation over published metadata; the LLM layer only extracts and summarises breaking-change statements from changelog text, and every statement it emits is anchored to a quoted changelog line. A3 (when unsure): findings are tiered by provenance — 'declared' (from requires_php/tested/requires fields, hard facts), 'changelog-stated' (quoted verbatim), and 'community-reported' (forum-derived, always shown with the source thread and a lower confidence band). Where the engine cannot reach a verdict it says 'no evidence either way for this pair' rather than inventing a conflict, and the safe-order recommendation degrades to 'apply nothing today, these three are unverifiable'. It never opens a ticket, never contacts a plugin author, never escalates to a person. A4: all sources are free public JSON on their own refresh cadence with hash/timestamp gates, as above. A5: nightly full crawl of the plugin index, hourly delta on customer site inventories, and a canary check that a known-good fixture site produces its known-good report before any new index is promoted. A6: zero human minutes — the product's entire output is a report and an ordering.
time_to_first_revenue: 2-4 weeks. The lead magnet is free and self-selling: connect your sites and get an instant list of which specific client sites run abandoned, vulnerable, or PHP-incompatible plugins. It converts because it names client sites the agency is responsible for. No outbound qualification, no demo.
risks: Adjacent incumbents already sell a strictly better answer to part of this: WP Remote and WP Umbrella do sandbox/staging update testing at roughly $1.99-$19.99/site/mo, which empirically catches breakage a metadata engine can only predict. The honest positioning is portfolio-wide triage and ordering before you spend staging cycles, not a replacement for staging — and that is a narrower claim than run-1 assumed. The buyer is price-sensitive and churns. The community-conflict tier is the weakest evidence layer and the most likely source of false positives that erode trust fast.

name: WarmRadar
one_liner: One dashboard watching every client sending domain you run — spam rate, authentication, blacklists — that alerts you before a client's campaign silently dies in Gmail.
problem: Google's bulk-sender rules impose a 0.30% hard spam-complaint ceiling (0.10% target) on senders above 5,000 messages/day to Gmail, with SPF/DKIM/DMARC mandatory. Agencies run outbound for 10-100 SMB clients, each on separate sending domains and mailboxes; one broken DKIM record or one bursty ramp tanks a client's campaign for weeks before anyone notices — and that is the churn event in a business where retainers run $1,500-$8,000/month. The monitoring stack agencies actually use is Google Postmaster Tools (free, one domain at a time), MXToolbox, and $20-60/mo seed testers. Nothing aggregates across a client book, so 'no data' and 'no problem' look identical.
target_customer: Cold-email and outbound lead-gen agencies of 2-30 people running Smartlead/Instantly/Apollo across many separate client sending domains; secondarily in-house SDR teams operating multi-domain sending infrastructure.
revenue_model: Self-serve monthly SaaS tiered by monitored domains. The agency connects domains via Google Postmaster API OAuth plus a DNS TXT verification; alerts route to Slack and email. Card at signup, Stripe dunning.
pricing_hypothesis: $199/mo up to 25 domains, $499/mo up to 100, $999/mo up to 500. Anchored explicitly against one prevented churn event of a $1,500-$8,000/mo retainer client — the tool pays for its whole year by saving a single account.
knowledge_base: Entirely API-native and continuously self-refreshing, with no curated content at all. (1) The Google Postmaster Tools API — a public REST service at gmailpostmastertools.googleapis.com with v1 plus v2/v2beta (v2 reached GA on 3 Feb 2026, adding domainStats.batchQuery and domain compliance-status endpoints), exposing spam rate, domain and IP reputation, delivery errors and authentication success rates per domain per day. (2) Live DNS: SPF, DKIM selector, DMARC, MTA-STS and BIMI record fetch and policy parse, plus DMARC aggregate (RUA) report ingestion when the agency points RUA at us. (3) Public DNSBL/RBL queries per sending IP and domain. (4) The published bulk-sender requirement thresholds themselves (Google, Yahoo, Microsoft), diffed on a weekly schedule. Staleness detection is intrinsic and is the product's most important honesty feature: every metric carries a source timestamp, Postmaster data lags 1-2 days by design, and the UI shows a per-domain 'last good pull' — marking a domain 'blind' rather than 'healthy' when a pull fails or the domain falls below Postmaster's reporting volume floor.
autonomy_case: A1: sign up, OAuth Postmaster, add domains, alerts begin — no call, no onboarding session, card charged at signup and renewed automatically. A2: the deliverable is a computed status and a threshold alert; nothing is authored or reviewed by a person. A3 (when unsure): degradation is the core design. A domain below Postmaster's volume floor genuinely has no spam-rate data, and the product says 'blind: below Gmail's reporting threshold' instead of showing a green check. Remediation guidance is a deterministic checklist keyed to the specific failing signal (missing DKIM selector, DMARC p=none, IP listed on a named DNSBL) with the raw record shown — never an opinion, never a routed ticket, never a human. A4: every source is an API or a live DNS query refreshing on its own cadence with zero curation. A5: per-domain polling crons with per-source circuit breakers; a failed pull marks the domain stale and pages the customer's own alert channel with 'monitoring degraded' rather than silently continuing to report healthy. A6: bounded — onboarding is OAuth plus DNS verification, both self-service with an in-app verification checker.
time_to_first_revenue: 2-4 weeks. The free 'audit your whole client book' scan needs only DNS and blacklist lookups (no OAuth, no signup friction), reliably surfaces at least one genuinely broken record in any book of 20+ domains, and that finding is the close. Agencies are an easily list-able cold-outreach target and cluster in known communities.
risks: Single-point dependency on Google: v1 is being retired in favour of v2 with breaking schema changes, and Google can restrict or alter the API unilaterally — the product's core signal is not ours. The category is filling in (MailReach, GlockApps, Suped, plus Smartlead's own deliverability add-ons), so the defensible slice is specifically multi-client aggregation and the blind-versus-healthy honesty, not the underlying signals. Agencies churn hard and the customer base itself is volatile; a customer losing clients shrinks their tier.

name: NexusPilot
one_liner: Connect your stores and NexusPilot tells you the day you cross a state's economic-nexus threshold — and never touches your filings.
problem: Remote sellers owe registration once they cross a state's economic-nexus threshold, and the thresholds are moving right now: seventeen states had eliminated the 200-transaction test as of 1 Aug 2026 (Illinois on 1 Jan 2026, Kentucky on 1 Aug 2026), which increases exposure for low-volume high-ticket sellers who were previously safe under the transaction prong. Most sub-$3M multi-channel sellers do not know where they stand until a state finds them, because the incumbent tools are priced and positioned for sellers who already need full filing automation.
target_customer: Solo and small-team multi-channel sellers doing roughly $100k-$3M/yr on Shopify, Amazon, Etsy and WooCommerce who are past single-state comfort but nowhere near wanting a filing and remittance platform.
revenue_model: Self-serve flat monthly SaaS connected via store OAuth. Monitoring and alerting only — explicitly not registration, not filing, not remittance. Stripe subscription with automated dunning; install via the Shopify App Store or direct signup.
pricing_hypothesis: $29/mo single store, $59/mo up to 5 stores/channels. Deliberately positioned as a cheap insurance line below the tier where TaxJar's real multi-state support begins, and priced so it never competes with the filing platforms it hands data off to.
knowledge_base: Two halves with different refresh mechanics, and the product is explicit about which is which. The live half is the customer's own order data — Shopify/Amazon/Etsy/Woo APIs polled continuously, with per-state rolling revenue and transaction counts computed on each state's own measurement period (calendar year versus trailing twelve months differ by state). The rules half is a ~46-row table of thresholds, measurement periods, marketplace-facilitator treatment and effective dates. It is small but must not rot, so a weekly scheduled job fetches each state DOR's remote-seller page plus the Streamlined Sales Tax governing board's per-state certificates of compliance and a small set of dated public trackers (Avalara publishes and date-stamps a transaction-threshold tracker, last updated 3 Aug 2026), hashes each source, and flags any state whose source changed for automated re-extraction. Every state row displays 'verified as of <date>'; a row whose sources have not been confirmed in 30 days flips to 'unverified — do not rely' and its alerts are suppressed rather than fired against possibly-stale rules.
autonomy_case: A1: Shopify App Store install or web OAuth, card, exposure map in minutes; renewal is automatic and cancellation is in-app. A2: threshold tracking is arithmetic over the seller's own orders — nothing is drafted, nothing is reviewed. A3 (when unsure): the product deliberately makes a narrow, dated claim — 'your Illinois sales crossed $100,000 on 2026-07-14 under rules we verified on <date>; this is a monitoring signal, not tax advice, and physical presence or marketplace-facilitator treatment can change the answer.' Where a state's rules are unverified, or where the seller's channel mix means marketplace-facilitated sales may or may not count toward the threshold (a genuine per-state ambiguity), it shows both computations side by side and refuses to pick one. It never files, never registers, and never hands the user to a person: the only escalation it offers is 'here are the filing platforms, and here is your data exported for them.' A4: the live half is fully automatic; the rules half is scheduled-diff with explicit per-row staleness and fail-closed suppression. A5: order-sync cron with backfill on reconnect, and a rules-refresh job that fails closed to 'unverified'. A6: zero human minutes; the only support surface is OAuth reconnection.
time_to_first_revenue: 2-4 weeks. Shopify App Store distribution plus a free tier that shows the exposure map for one state and paywalls the rest. The alert itself ('you are at 82% of the Texas threshold') is the conversion event, so acquisition and conversion are the same automated motion.
risks: The weakest A4 in this set: the threshold table is extracted from human-readable state pages, and while the diff-and-flag mechanism makes staleness detectable, the extraction itself still has to be right and there is no authoritative machine-readable feed for all 46 jurisdictions. The category is crowded above and below (TaxCloud, Kintsugi, Numeral, TaxJar) and Shopify ships its own free built-in nexus tracker, which is a real substitute. The low price point makes volume the only path, and 'monitoring without filing' risks being seen as an incomplete product customers outgrow within a year — churn by graduation.

name: LicenseWatch
one_liner: LicenseWatch checks every technician on your roster against the state's own license file every night and reports what the state actually says: active, expired, or unverifiable.
problem: A lapsed technician licence stops permit pulls, can void job insurance on an active project, and is discovered at the worst possible moment. Shops track this in spreadsheets fed by whatever the tech last told the office, so the spreadsheet says 'current' while the state's record says 'expired'. LicensedTrades.com already sells this job self-serve at $199/$349/$599/$1,199 per month with a 14-day no-card trial — proving both the buyer and the price band — but it tracks customer-entered data, so it faithfully reproduces the same lie. REFRAMING (explicit): the run-1 cluster (TradeCred, StateReady, LicenseIQ, License Radar, Renewly, StateSwitch, LicenseStack, StormClear) all fail A4 because their core asset is a hand-curated 50-state map of CE hours, bonds, reciprocity and application steps — data with no machine-readable source and no self-detecting staleness — and several fail A2 by bundling 'we file the application for you' concierge work. The minimal reframe is to delete the requirement-advice and concierge layers entirely and keep only assertions a state's own published licence file can prove: status, expiry date, licence classification, disciplinary flag. Everything else is reported as 'unverified'.
target_customer: Electrical, HVAC, plumbing and roofing contractors with 5-100 licensed technicians, especially multi-state and storm-restoration shops; secondarily staffing agencies placing licensed trades across state lines.
revenue_model: Self-serve monthly SaaS tiered by technicians monitored. Upload a roster CSV (name, licence number, state), get nightly verification against state files, expiry alerts at 90/60/30/7 days, and a bid-ready compliance export PDF. Card at signup, Stripe dunning.
pricing_hypothesis: $99/mo up to 15 techs, $249/mo up to 50, $499/mo up to 150 — undercutting LicensedTrades' verified $199/$349/$599/$1,199 ladder while selling a strictly stronger claim: state-verified rather than self-reported.
knowledge_base: State licensing authorities that publish bulk or queryable licence data, refreshed on each state's own cadence. Verified during this screen: Texas TDLR publishes 152 downloadable CSV licence files at tdlr.texas.gov/LicenseSearch/licfile.asp — including per-trade files for electricians and air-conditioning technicians/contractors — alongside a published record layout (lrformat.txt); California CSLB publishes a list-of-licenses download; Florida DBPR and roughly 15-25 further boards publish comparable extracts or lookup endpoints. Each state file is fetched on schedule, row-counted and content-hashed; a file that shrinks materially, or fails to change past its expected cadence, marks that entire state 'stale', and every technician in it flips to 'unverified as of <date>' — never to 'compliant'. Coverage is a first-class number in the UI ('we can verify 6 of your 9 states'), which doubles as the honest sales pitch and keeps the product from overclaiming.
autonomy_case: A1: signup, roster CSV upload, first verification run the same night; card at signup, renewal automatic. A2: record matching and date arithmetic against state files — no human confirms a match or reviews a result. A3 (when unsure): exactly three states are ever displayed — verified-active, verified-not-active, and unverified. A fuzzy name match below threshold returns 'we found 2 possible records for this licence number and we will not pick one' and shows both records with their source rows. The product never advises what CE to take, never fills an application, and never routes to a licensing agency or a human. A4: state-published files on schedule with hash and row-count staleness detection, as above — this is the entire point of the reframe. A5: per-state ingestion crons with independent circuit breakers; a state failing three consecutive fetches fires a 'coverage degraded' notice to affected customers rather than silently serving last week's answer as current. A6: zero human minutes; roster upload is a templated CSV with a column mapper.
time_to_first_revenue: 3-5 weeks. The free roster audit — paste ten licence numbers, we tell you what the state says — is self-selling because it routinely contradicts the shop's own spreadsheet. The state licence files themselves double as a cold-outreach list of contractors with licence classes and addresses, so lead generation is the same pipeline as the product.
risks: Coverage is the whole product and it is uneven: some boards publish nothing in bulk, some rate-limit, some change file formats without notice, and 'we can only verify 12 states' is a hard objection against LicensedTrades' claim to cover all of them — even though that claim rests on self-reported data. Deliberately dropping CE and reciprocity guidance removes the half of the value some buyers actually want, and may cap the price. A few boards' terms of use restrict bulk reuse and must be checked state by state. Willingness to pay here is preventive rather than urgent, so the buying trigger is weak outside an active lapse — this is the softest demand signal of the seven.

name: UnderwaterRx
one_liner: UnderwaterRx reads your pharmacy's remittance file every week, compares every fill to CMS's published acquisition cost, and shows exactly which claims were reimbursed below cost and how long you have to appeal.
problem: Independent pharmacies are routinely reimbursed below acquisition cost and mostly cannot say which specific fills, because catching it means joining every line of a remittance file against a drug-cost benchmark. This just became a legal question with a number attached: from 1 Jan 2026 Colorado requires PBMs to reimburse rural independent pharmacies at or above NADAC plus a dispensing fee, and New Jersey's bill sets a commercial floor of NADAC plus the state Medicaid professional dispensing fee. Practitioners report that most pharmacies still have not executed the statutory appeal process in alignment with their state's requirements — so laws with teeth go unused for want of the detection step. REFRAMING (explicit): run-1's MacGuard fails A1/A2/A3 in three places — contingency pricing on recovered dollars (payment depends on a negotiated outcome, not a self-serve purchase), 'we write your audit appeals' as a service, and PBM audit defence, which is human advocacy by construction. The minimal reframe is flat subscription only; the product detects and documents, and generates the appeal as a downloadable document the pharmacist submits through the PBM's own portal. It never files, never negotiates, never touches audit defence. That also swaps the moat from PBM-specific MAC lists (not machine-readable) to CMS NADAC, which is weekly, public, machine-readable, and is precisely what the new state reimbursement-floor statutes key on.
target_customer: Owners of independent retail pharmacies (1-5 locations) in states with a NADAC-referenced reimbursement floor or a statutory MAC-appeal right — the NCPA and PSAO membership base, roughly 19,000 stores nationally with the addressable subset defined by state law.
revenue_model: Flat monthly SaaS per location, fully self-serve. Upload or auto-import the remittance/claims export; get a weekly underwater report and generated appeal documents. No contingency, no percentage of recovery, no engagement letter.
pricing_hypothesis: $149/mo per location, $99/location at three or more. Priced flat and low precisely so it needs no negotiation and no ROI approval, and so a single correctly-appealed claim covers a month.
knowledge_base: CMS NADAC via the data.medicaid.gov metastore API, verified live: sixteen NADAC datasets are exposed, with the current-year 'NADAC (National Average Drug Acquisition Cost) 2026' dataset carrying a modified timestamp of 2026-08-11 at the time of this check — i.e. it genuinely refreshes weekly, the cadence the statutes assume. Joined to the FDA NDC directory (public, machine-readable) for product identity, and to a small curated table of state reimbursement-floor and MAC-appeal statutes with their appeal windows — the only hand-maintained element, diffed weekly against state DOI and board pages such as Colorado DOI's PBM legislation guidance page. Staleness detection is the safety-critical control: every report is stamped with the NADAC file's effective week, and if the current NADAC file is more than 10 days old the app refuses to publish new underwater findings and states that the benchmark is stale, rather than comparing a fill against a superseded week — because a wrong week produces a wrong dollar gap and a wrong appeal.
autonomy_case: A1: signup, card, upload the remittance export, first report inside one session; renewal automatic, cancel in-app. A2: the comparison is arithmetic (reimbursement versus NADAC x quantity plus dispensing fee) and the appeal document is templated from the statute's required elements plus the claim's own fields — no human reviews or advocates. A3 (when unsure): an NDC absent from that week's NADAC file (common for new and specialty products) returns 'no published benchmark for this NDC in the week of <date> — not evaluated', never an inferred gap. Where the PBM contract rate rather than the statutory floor governs, the product names which claims it cannot judge and why. It presents a document for the pharmacist to file and states plainly that it is not filing, not appealing and not representing them; it never routes to a consultant or an attorney. A4: CMS publishes NADAC weekly to a public API, FDA NDC is public, and the statute table is small and diff-monitored with per-row verified-as-of dates. A5: weekly NADAC ingest with an effective-date guard, per-file row-count sanity check, and a hard block on report generation whenever the benchmark is stale. A6: zero human minutes; the file format is the only support surface, mitigated by shipping parsers for the common pharmacy management system exports.
time_to_first_revenue: 4-6 weeks — the slowest of these seven, because it needs a remittance parser per pharmacy management system and the buyer is reached through associations rather than an app store. Offsetting that: the free 'upload one month, see your underwater dollars' report is unusually self-evident, and the state statutes attach a dated appeal deadline that creates real urgency.
risks: Remittance and claims export formats vary by pharmacy management system and are the real engineering cost; a bad parser looks like a wrong dollar figure, which destroys trust instantly and permanently in this buyer. NADAC is a survey average of acquisition cost, not the pharmacy's actual invoice cost, so 'below cost' is a defensible proxy rather than a proof — the copy must be careful or it overpromises. The statutory floors are new, state-limited and contested, so the addressable base is smaller than 'all independent pharmacies', and PBM contract terms govern instead of the statute on many claims. The independent pharmacy population is also shrinking, which caps the market's trajectory.
